speechtext:
Bill (No. 106) to amend the Post Office Act (the Postmaster General) read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1,
What is the object of removing these officers from the provisions of the Civil Service Act ?

By the Civil Service Act

they are required to undergo a preliminary examination and it is intended to discontinue this system and substitute the departmental examination. It was not considered of any practical importance that these officers should be required to have special qualifications necessary to pass the examination required by the civil service examiners. A more practical examination would probably be better.
What would be the nature of the examination ?

That would be for the department to prescribe. It would be such an examination that would call for a knowledge of the elementary subjects, such as reading and writing and a little arithmetic, in order to see if they have the necessary education to enable them to discharge the duties of their office.
That is practically the examination that they are called on to pass now.

In the first place, they will not have to pay anything. At present a very large number of persons present themselves annually for examination who are never called to any position, but under this Bill no man will be requested to undergo an examination unless there is a position for him. It will be the same practice as is followed in the Toronto police corps, I presume. Under the present law, thousands of persons have presented themselves at the annual examinations, at considerable cost to themselves, and the great majority of them never receive an appointment.

This Bill will afford opportunities to the department to pass those whom they wish to pass, whether eligible or not. I think that the system of submitting these young men for examination to some entirely independent board, where each applicant stands on his own merits, is much better than to leave the department to select those to whom they wish to give appointments and exclude those whom they do not want to pass.

This Bill will take that branch of the service altogether out of the operation of the Civil Service Act. It will be excluded, not simply in respect of examinations, but of everything else. This brings up the question of the terms of employment. Under the Civil Service Act these men are yearly employees, getting yearly salaries, but under this Bill their salary will be so much per day, and it does not provide how many hours will constitute a day's work. If we are to change from the yearly system to the day system, we should define how many hours constitute a day's work, and will entitle a man to a day's pay. It seems to me that eight hours work in the eleven between 7 a.m. and 6 p.m. should be the limit. It is an essential principle of 127*
employment by the day, that the number of hours should be defined. A man might work a sufficient number of hours in a day to entitle him to two day's pay. That cannot be the case under the present system, under which the employees are paid by the month or the year.

There is nothing in the law to-day defining what should be the length of a day's work. It seems to me it is equally necessary to pass a rule in the one case as in the other, if it be necessary at all. There is nothing to show that there has been any abuse as regards overwork in the branch I have to do with. Some people have very exaggerated ideas of the labour exacted from many of these officials. So far as the length of the day is concerned, the only class that takes exception to this measure is the letter carriers. I had an account taken of their labour, and I find that the average day of the letter carriers on duty throughout Canada is eight hours and twenty-one minutes. There will be no enlargement of that day, and there is no necessity for any statutory provision on the subject.

Can the hon. minister give us the particulars respecting the information he has collected as to the length of day? These men have to go to the post office in the morning to get the letters and put them in shipshape before beginning delivery. Is that time included ?
I understand that the eight hours and twenty-one minutes includes all the time they are on duty.

If that be the case, it ought to be easily arranged to have the number of hours specified in this Bill. At present there is no specified number of hours. The employees are under the monthly wage system, under which a man does what work there is to be done, and will sometimes have longer and sometimes shorter days. But when we change to the day system, we are paying so much money for so many hours work, and the question is how many hours work should be in the'day. If a man does ten hour's work, that would amount to $2.50 at 25 cents per hour. We should either have the one system or the other. If we introduce the day labour system, we should specify the number of hours per day.

Many letter carriers are very uneasy as to what their position will be after this Bill becomes law. This Bill puts them on day work. They regard their positions as of a permanent character, and they are very uneasy as to whether they will simply be in the position of men employed for the day, whose services may be dispensed with to-morrow.

The measure will in no way whatever weaken

their tenure of office. There is a clause in the measure saying that they shall be removable only by Order in Council. That is all the guarantee that any one in the civil service has, and there is no more possibility of their being dismissed without cause under this provision than under the existing condition of affairs. I am not aware of any parliament having fixed by law what shall be the particular hours constituting a day's work. My hon. friend (Mr. Barker) may know of some case of that kind and if so. I would like to hear of it. The postal departments may. as a matter of policy, name a number of hours in their regulations, but I am not aware of any legislative body or parliament binding its hands in that way.
Will the Postmaster General allow a question ?
Yes, with pleasure.

I understood the hon. gentleman to say that, at present, under the Civil Service Act these officials could be dismissed only by Order in Council, and that hereafter they would have the same protection. But, this Act declares that it shall supersede the Civil Service Act.

But; iu clause 12 of this Act it is provided :
Appointments, promotions, reductions in grade and dismissals under this Act shall be made by the Governor in Council.
What practice obtains in the United States respecting the hours of employment of letter carriers ?
I am not familiar with the American practice.

The objection I see to fixing the hours of labour to a day's work is that the men have a certain beat in which to discharge their duties and an active man can probably do his work in six or seven hours, while a slower man will take eight or nine hours. To keep all employed for the same length of time, it will be necessary to make the beats for some men at least 25 per cent greater than for others. A man exercising diligence in the pursuit of his business can lessen the number of hours to a considerable extent. If the average is now, as the Postmaster General has said, eight hours and twenty-one minutes, that is not too long a day's work.

That may be an argument why the staff should be left under the present Civil Service Act, which allows and provides for all that. But we are adopting a new policy, a new principle altogether, and it seems to me that it is absolutely necessary that the number of hours' work should be specified and limited. I think it should be eight hours within eleven, which would give two or three hours a day when the men are not required on the beat.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General

speechtext: What action would the Postmaster General be compelled to take if a man could not do an ordinary day's work in eight hours ?
If an ordinary man could not do the work it would be necessary to engage more than one ordinary man for the work.

In what respect is the Civil Service Act so defective that the Postmaster General introduces this Bill ? This seems to be rather in the line of discrediting the Civil Service Act and taking a large number from under it that were intended originally to be under the provisions of that Act.
My hon. friend only sees what he thinks are the bad spots in this Bill. I hope he will be able to see something good in it.
We do.

I will try to point out some of the good points. This is not forced upon anybody now in the service. It applies to those to be appointed hereafter, but gives those now in the service the privilege of availing themselves of it, if they think it is to their advantage; but if they do not think so, they are left in the full enjoyment of their rights. Now, I have not heard any complaints from any of the classes in question, with the exception of the letter carriers. Let me state what the position of the letter carriers is to-day. As far back as 1872, the law with regard to the appointment for letter carriers provided that their initial salary should; be $300 a year, with an annual increase of $40 until a maximum of $500-or a possible maximum of $600 under certain conditions-was attained. That continued to be the rate until 1874. On the change of government in 1874, a change was made in the initial salary, the Mackenzie government fixing the amount at $400. No other changes were made at that time. That continued to be the law until the downfall Orf the Mackenzie government. When the new government came into office, they reduced the initial salary to from $400 to $300 a year. That reduction continued in force from 1878 until 1882, when the then government made a change reducing the annual increase from $40 to $30, and confirming the reduction of initial salary from $400 to $300. Iu 1885 they increased the initial salary from $300 to $360, leaving the annual increase at $30. This continued from 1885 up to the present time. In the public interest it is advisable that there should be some incentive to letter carriers to report for duty when duty calls. The public expect their mail to be delivered to them with regularity. But this cannot be accomplished if when the letter carriers should appear for duty on a given morning a considerable number of them are absent. Experience has shown that those who are

on yearly pay are absent very much more often than those who are on day's pay. It becomes necessary sometimes to engage persons to act as letter carriers, who are not eligible to be appointed under the Civil Service Act. They discharge the same duties as those appointed under the Civil Service Act and their pay is, perhaps, slightly less. Good men taken on in that position are allowed to continue and my information is that those who are on the civil service list are absent from duty three times as long per annum-over and above the statutory holidays-as those who are on by the day. The day's pay is an incentive to them to report for duty. I understand that in England the same principle obtains, and if a letter carrier does not appear for duty at the proper time he loses his day's pay or a great portion of it. There are substitutes appointed and the letter carrier suffers a pecuniary loss because of his absence. X do not know how it is in the United States, but, perhaps, my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) is informed on that point.

The information I have is very limited, but I was going to say after what had been stated by the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) with regard to the reduction of hours, that I understand [DOT]there are two staffs delivering, beginning earlier and continuing later, and that the men work eight hours a day. I am not sure, however, that such is the case.

At all events there is a manifest advantage in having some means of exerting pressure upon this class of officers, so that they shall appear at the time of duty. It is as essential for them as for the trainmen to appear when required. They are required to perform a class of duty the regularity of which is, all important, and we are frequently embarrassed because letter carriers at the last moment fail to appear at the time appointed. It is necessary to meet that weak point in the service, and a measure of this kind is in the public interest in that respect alone. Now I have said that this measure is in other respects an advantage to the employees. For example, I have had a statement prepared by the officers to show the difference between the salaries received under the present law and those which will be received under the proposed law. Take the case of. a letter carrier to-day entering the service. As the law has been for about the last twenty years, entering at $360 a year, his salary increasing at $30 a year until he attains the maximum of $600, he will enter upon his ninth year before he will attain the maximum of $600. Under the proposed measure he will enter as a probationer for a period of six months, he will be learning the route and the small matters they have to learn. At the end of six months he is supposed to be qualified to be confirmed in his position. During that probationery period he is under instructions, we have to detail a man, so to speak, to teach him, not necessarily go with him all the time ; but he is under tutelage for a time. Nevertheless during that period of tutelage he is paid $1.20 a day for six months. As soon as he is qualified to be confirmed in his appointment he then begins his salary of $1.50 a day, which amounts to $469.50 per annum. We give him two weeks leave of absence, and at the expiration of two years his pay goes up to $547.75 a year. At the end of those two years he will be entitled to promotion, assuming always that he has deserved it, to $2 a day, or $626 a year. His salary will remain at $626 unless he should be promoted or reduced in rank. Assuming he remains at $626, when he has entered upon his ninth year of service, an officer appointed under this law will have received during that period from the commencement, $713.50 more than under the present law. In addition to this there is a provision that a letter carrier may get every year a bonus of 10 days extra holidays where his conduct has been reasonably satisfactory. It does not mean that there is a prize only to the top man, but I am hoping that a number of men in the service will win this 10 days extra holidays, or he may at his option receive $2 a day, or $20, in lieu of these extra ten days.
Do you strike off his pay for each day's absence ?

Now if he should accept $20 a year in lieu of the holidays, he would receive during that comparative period that I have referred to, $883.50 more under this proposed measure than under the existing law, or an average without the bonus of $20 a year, of $83.94, and with the bonus of $20 a year, an average of $103.94 more than under the present law.
What about superannuation ?

The Superannuation Act was repealed some years ago, and the Retirement Act has been adopted in lieu of it. They are living under the Retirement Act, and that is wholly for their benefit, not for the benefit of the country.

The hon. gentleman was making a comparison of the condition of the letter carriers under his law, and the conditions under the old law. Will he give us an idea of how much better off these men will be in respect to superannuation?

It is not necessary to discuss a repealed Act; if the hon. gentleman will ask me to discuss the Retirement Act I will be glad to do so. The Retirement Act is now in force as to all new appointees and all appointees of recent years, so that the Superannuation Act each year is having less and less application, and

if this Act was to drop it would not affect anybody, either under the Superannuation or the Retirement Acts.
When the hon. gentleman was speaking of the salary, I asked if he made any provision for striking off from their salary for days they were absent, and he did not deign to answer.

Because the question was not applicable to my observations, and would have been more fittingly asked at a latter period. At the same time I would say to the hon. gentleman that the Bill provides for payment of a day's work, it also gives the men two weeks leave of absence. I believe the hon. gentleman is an employer of labour himself, as I am sure many of us in this House are, and he knows something about fines, rates of pay, and so forth. Perhaps the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) will tell us whether he considers these rates will be regarded in his part of the world as reasonable to be paid by the taxpayers of Canada.
I think that is merely evading the question. 1 asked what I regarded as a proper and a courteous question.
I have answered the question.
If the minister does not choose to reply he need not do so. The answer he has given is no answer at all.
The hon. gentleman asked me if there is a provision made for leave of absence.
I asked whether there was a provision made for a reduction of their wages when they were absent.

As I explained, they are paid for the time they work. That is a system perfectly easy to understand. A man is paid so much per day for the time he works, he is also paid for two weeks that he does not work, and may be paid for ten days further that he does not work. If he is absent more days than that, his pay is stopped during the additional period of absence.

I want to remind the minister', when he wants members on this side to be courteous to him, that when he was on this side of the House himself he did not draw the line so closely, and he was not very courteous.

I hope I have improved my methods.
Mr. qOCHRANE. Not much.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. What about cases of sickness ?

I was about to say when I began my observations, that no class of officials except letter Hon. Mr. MULOCK.
carriers take exception to this measure, and inasmuch as those who object to it are not bound by it, I hardly see that they have much standing. I happen to have received yesterday the following communication which shows another side to this question : Toronto, April 26, 1902. Hon. Wm. Mulock, P.M.G.
Dear Sir,-At a meeting of the employees of the Toronto post office including porters, messengers, box collectors and mail transfer agents, it was unanimously agreed that your amendment to the Post Office Act is a move in the right direction and we would be glad to see it pass and will be pleased to come under the provisions contained therein.
Respectfully submitted.
Your obedient servants,
P. S. RUTTAN, Secretary (pro tem), W. J. RAY, Chairman.
You do not know where the meeting was held In Toronto ?
I know nothing except .what the communication says.
Does it refer to the letter carriers being pleased ?
I have read every word of it. Shall I read it again?
If you please.

(reading)
Toronto, April 26, 1902. Hon. Wm. Mulock, P.M.G.,
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-At a meeting of the employees of the Toronto Post Office Department including porters, messengers, box collectors and mail transfer agents, it was unanimously agreed that your amendment to the Post Office Act is a move iu the right direction and we would be glad to see it pass and will be pleased to come under the provisions contained therein.
They have the option of coming In or not coming In.
That does not include the letter carriers because it says nothing about them.
I am not speaking for the letter carriers. I am explaining that I have heard from all these employees except the letter carriers. As to the others they have sent me this communication.
You do not know how many were present at the meeting ?

I have told the hon. gentleman that the document contains all the information I possess on the subject.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. My hon. friend has not answered my question in regard to cases of sickness. Employees should lose their pay, of course, if they are absent from work, but in cases of sickness will they be deprived of their pay ?

The law makes no provision for their being pain when they are not at work, except for two weeks annual leave and for ten days additional pay as bonus.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Does not my hon. friend think it would be unfair to make them lose their pay if they are sick ?

Well, the ten days bonus will more than pay them for that. During the year gone by statistics have been collected and they show that the ten days bonus that we give them will quite pay for absences from other causes than holidays.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. So that they will have to get sick during these ten days, or otherwise they will lose their pay ?
That will be for their election. This will cure a great many of sickness.

If they get pay now during sickness and they are to be deprived of that pay under the provisions of this Bill they will not be in as good a position. They get pay now if they can get a medical certificate, but under the provisions of this Bill, they will be deprived of pay during the time they are sick. Am I right in saying that ?

I have explained that they are paid for the days they work, and they are paid for fourteen days holidays when they do not work. They are also paid a ten days bonus, and as to the rest if they do not work other days, they are not paid for other days, whatever be the cause of absence. The civil service is very bad for the health at times. We find a great many absent when pay goes on who might perhaps be able to do their work if pay did not go on. We have had numerous cases of rapid recovery when it was made clear that longer absence would be accompanied by loss of pay. I was about to give the committee some information as to the rates of pay in other walks of life for people who are more or less in the public service. Take the case of policemen. I have a schedule showing the rates of pay of that class of people. In the city of Brantford the rate of pay is $1.30 per day for me first year, increasing to $1.40 the next year, and then, in the fourth year, to $1.50, after ten years $1.60 and after sixteen years $1.70 per day. They receive no pension, they work nine hours a day and receive uniforms.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: They have lots of pickings.

I should be sorry to think that of them. I think they are a highly respectable body of men. In Hamilton the policemen receive $1.40 a day at appointment, after one year $1.80, and after six years $1.90 per day. They have the benefit of the police benefit fund, their hours
of work are eight hours a day and they receive uniforms, except shoes and underclothing. In Kingston policemen receive $35 a month upon entrance, and $40 a month after. They receive uo pensions but they are granted $45 per annum as a clothing allowance. They work twelve hours a day. In London they deceive $1.40 a day on entrance, $1.55 after a year, and $1.90, usually, after three or four years. They are entitled to the police benefit fund, they receive uniforms, but no boots or underclothing, and they work eight hours during day duty, and nine hours during night duty. In Montreal they receive $9.20 per week on entrance, $10.20 after one year, $11.20 after three years and $12.20 a week for specially good men. They are entitled to share in the Police Benefit Society fund and they receive uniforms. They work twelve hours a day, six hours of inside and six hours of outside duty.
What about sick pay at these different places ?
I have no information here as to that.
You did not get the information on that ?

There is nothing in regard to that.
Mr. [DOT]CLARKE. Is that a return from the Labour Department ?

No. In Ottawa policemen receive $35 per month for three months and after three months $40, after one year $45 and after that $50, $55, or $60 on recommendation. They receive uniforms, no pension, work ten and a quarter hours day duty, and eight and three-quarters hours night duty. In Toronto they receive $1.30 a day on appointment, $1.50 after one year, with good conduct ;	$1.75,
after three years. That $1.75 continues until the end of seven years after which the pay is $2 per day. They receive half pay after 25 years service. They work eight hours a day which can be extended when necessary. In St. John they get $1.40 a day upon entrance.
Will the hon. Postmaster General allow me to interrupt him ? WTbat did he say in regard to the pay in Toronto ?
They get $2 a day after seven years service.
Well, there is a further provision for increase of pay after a given number of years.
I have not that. What is it ?
They get ten cents a day additional for each good conduct mark.
How long do they serve before receiving good conduct pay ?

I cannot remember that. Besides, this pay of $2 is for seven days in the week.
The POSTM ' >TER GENERAL. Well, the good conduct stripe may be a good feature.
What has all this information to do with the Bill ?

It is to show the committee what is paid in other walks of life. In St. John they get $1.40 on entrance, $1.50 after three years, and 81.60 after six years. They are on duty twelve hours in day time and ten hours at night. In Winnipeg the pay is $50 per month on entrance, $60 after one year, $65 after two years, $70 after three years; no pension; they get two full uniforms; work nine hours a day. In Vancouver the pay is $60 a month, increased to $70 after the first year. They receive two uniforms a year and equipment, work nine hours, including one hour for luncheon. It says a pension fund will be shortly established. In Halifax the pay is $400 a year, increased to $450 after one year's service, and they receive full uniforms and work ten hours a day.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Where did the Postmaster General get these statistics ?
My department wrote to the different cities for them.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Has the Postmaster General gathered all the facts? Can he tell us whether when a constable is off duty on account of sick leave, his pay is docked, as in the case of the post office service?
I have no information on that point.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
When you get the statistics you should get all the facts, so as to make a fair comparison.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. What comparison is
there between policemen and letter carriers; irrespective of salaries, of course?
They both have to walk.
Some people might think that a policeman's duties were altogether more onerous and hazardous.
They have different beats from the letter carriers.

The letter carriers work, as a rule, during the day time, and policemen are on duty at night often. I should think that if a man had a choice of serving as a letter carrier or as a policeman, the pay being equal, no doubt he would be a letter carrier. I think this because we are deluged with applications for the position of letter carrier, and they are often from men who have good callings; not unskilled men, but men who have trades.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext:
Why do they come to the government service when they have a trade of their own ? They evidently admire some features of it. There is constant employment, regularity of occupation, and their employer is sure to be able to pay them.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. That is the reason why I tell my hon. friend that he makes a grave mistake in comparing letter carriers to policemen.

In
what way ?
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Because it shows that in most cases the policemen are better off than the letter carriers.
The	POSTMASTER	GENERAL.	It
shows altogether the other way.
Mr. TAYLOR, Might I ask the hon. gentleman why he makes the law in reference to letter carriers and mail clerks different from that of government employees in other departments. As I understand it, in the inside service, where persons are working by the day they are paid for seven days. The Minister of Agriculture told us the other night that in the census department the officials are being paid for seven days, and I think that is the rule in all the other departments. Why make a different rule for these hard-worked letter carriers, who have to be out rain or shine, perhaps ten or twelve hours a day, and who if they are sick, lose their day's pay.

I hope the Postmaster General does not think that we are only picking out the bad spots in this Bill. I have been carefully through the Rill and have compared it with the present system, and I am prepared to say that there are some good features to it, but at the same time it is our duty when in committee to pick out the bad spots. There is no doubt that the limitation of the time for reaching the maximum salary is a good feature in this Bill. The old system of $30 a year increase for nine years before a man reached the very low maximum was altogether absurd. If we can get some necessary amendments as regards the hours, and one or two other things in this Bill it will accomplish a great deal of good. One good feature is that it does away with Sunday work. As a matter of fact, at the present time in some cities, if not all, the letter carriers are brought to the office to do some kind of work on Sunday, but under this Bill the local officers will have to report if there is necessity for that, and they will be paid for Sunday. But better still, it will have the effect of doing away with Sunday work altogether, and that is a good feature. My own opinion, however, is that this Bill does not touch the right spot. The Postmaster General wishes to make his letter carrier staff more effective, and there is no doubt that an effective staff of letter carriers is
What is the matter with the system ?
The patronage system ; that is the matter with the system.
Does this Bill do away with that?

Not at all. A bad system does not produce good results, and I am not surprised to hear the Postmaster General say that there are weak spots in his staff. The very fact that a Bill of this kind is thought to be necesasry to cure some of the diseases is evidence that there is a bad system, and that it is producing bad results. I had hoped that the Postmaster General would have been able to take the bull by the horns in this case. An effective staff is necessary, and I thought that the hon. gentleman might be able to take the matter of appointing and governing the staff altogether out of the field of politics; and partisan politics at that. That is what makes the staff non-effective and inefficient. It is that that some men know they can be sick and they can play with the officials because they will be sustained by the influence they can bring to bear.
I would like the hon. gentleman (Mr. Puttee) to give us the information on which he bases his statement that this staff is inefficient.

I am only drawing what I think to be the proper inference from what the Postmaster General told us himself. He said that men paid by the day are only sick one-third as much as men working under the Civil Serive Act.
Do you state that is a fact yourself?
I heard the Postmaster General state it.
I stated it. I have information in my department to that effect.

Have you information to the effect that when men are employed by the month or year there is three times more sick leave than when they are employed by the day?
The POSTS1 ASTER GENERAL. These are statistics I have from the Toronto bffice.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
We should get the ministers working by the day.
The POSTS1ASTER GENERAL. And the members of parliament.
Is it not a fact that when a man is off sick he has to send a medical certificate to the department?

Certificates should be produced, but we very often find that these certificates are not wholly what they appear to be. Slen may be sick in reality, and yet they may have occasioned their own sickness. We have many instances, if your want details.
That often happens.

I am inclined to think, at all events, that there is some foundation for this opinion. I am not stating that the letter carrier staff is inefficient all through ; but, as a necessary result of the system, there are very weak spots in the operation of the service. The very fact that it is thought necessary to introduce a Bill of this kind, in order to get the men there every morning and not to have any misses, means that there have been misses in the past, and that as a matter of fact the staff is not as efficient as it would be under a better system. I thought we might possibly have a proposition to take this service away from the influence of politics altogether, and put it on a basis where merit and proper attention to work would be recognized and well paid. Now, there are some weak spots in this Bill, and if there are not some radical amendments made in it, I question very much whether it would not be better to keep to the Civil Service Act. For one thing, it does not state the hours which shall constitute a day's work. Then, it should include labourers, sorters and stampers. Then, subsection 2 of section 4 recognizes a new and bad principle, which I hope will be struck out of the Bill; that is, it provides that in the case of inefficiency, reductions in grade may be made.
That is not a change in the law.

It is a bad principle. This service consists wholly of manual labour, and we start on the very proper system of having men enter at the lowest grade and go up to the maximum. In labour of this kind, when a man is young, he is at his highest efficiency, and as he grows old he necessarily becomes less efficient, and this provision means that he is going down the ladder. It is a bad principle to recognize in an Act of parliament. If the man has performed his duties faithfully in the best years of his life, he should not be reduced in grade ; but he should be kept so long as he is able to do the work, and should then be superannuated. This provision should be made to read that in case of inefficient or unsatisfactory service or the committal of any offence against the rules, a man should be suspended as a penalty. That, it seems to me, would accomplish any object the Postmaster General has in view. But if we are going to leave the service under political influence, it is a bad principle to place in the hands of a minister the power to put a man down instead

of up. It is a principle to which I cannot agree.

I have taken considerable interest in this Bill and have given it careful study. One reason for that is that since I have had the honour of occupying a seat in this House, we have established in the city of Brantford a free letter delivery, and I naturally made myself conversant with that system, in order to see that the men employed were not overworked and were not underpaid ; and a great many of the letter carriers throughout the country have written to me asking me to look after their interests in this matter. Now, I can say, after a careful study of this Bill, that it establishes a system most favourable to the working classes, and the most liberal in its pay, of any that exists anywhere in the Dominion of Canada. There is no agricultural or machine or carpenter shop anywhere in this country where men are getting as good pay as these men will receive under this Bill, or where they work shorter hours.
The Bill applies to two classes of people-those who are trying to get into the government employ, and those now in it. Those that are in do not need to take the benefit of these provisions unless they like. Those that are without do not need to come under its provisions unless they want a government job. The first question is, how will the Bill affect those who are trying to get into the service ? At present a man is appointed at $1.15 a day, whereas under the Bill he will be appointed at $1.25, and he will be expected to act as probationer for a period of six months, during which time his pay will be $15 greater than it was under the old system. Under the old system a man was appointed at $360 per annum. Under the new system, after six months probation, he gets $469.50 per annum, or $109.50 more than under the old system. After the first year, under the present system, he gets $390. Under the new system he will get $409.50, or an increase of $79.50. At the end of the second year he can be put into grade ' C,' then his pay becomes $1.75 per day, or $547.75 per annum, which is $127.75 per annum more than he gets under the old system. In the fourth year, under the old system, he gets $450. while under the new system he gets $547.75, or an increase of $97.75. So that the man coming into the service will improve his position in four years by $414.50, and from that time he will be in receipt of $626 per annum.
Does the hon. member in his calculation provide that the employee shall work every day except Sunday ?

I am assuming that. As the Bill applies to those of the present staff who choose to come under these provisions, it has this effect upon all men who have been one, two, three, or four years in the service. If a man has been four years in the service he passes at once into class ' D.' Mr. PUTTEE.
which gives him $600 a year. If he has been five years in the service, and is drawing $480 a year at present, he will draw $626, or an increase of $146 a year. If he has been six years in the service, his wages will increase by $116 ; if he has been seven years in the service, they will increase by $86 ; if eight years, by $50 ; and if he is becoming a $600 man, the highest point to which he can reach under the present system, his wages will be $26 more. No injustice is done to anybody in that class, and the only man who has any cause of complaint at all is the man who is now getting $600 a year. This whole thing originated because a petition was sent in by the letter carriers for an increase of pay ; and the desire of the great majority of the employees of the Post Office Department has been gratified by this very radical increase. But it applies with less force to the class now getting $600 a year, and we have the right to ask whether $600 a year is not fair pay. We must not forget that there is another class into which a man may enter at the end of four years. By diligent service or by the discharge of especially arduous labour, he can be advanced to class ' E,' in which his wage is increased to $704.25 per annum.
I regard that as a very high rate of wages, higher than is paid in any manufacturing establishment in Canada to any class of employees no matter what years of apprenticeship they have to serve. In addition these post office employees get two weeks leave of absence, and under special circumstances that leave is extended ten days longer, equal to twenty dollars in money, besides getting clothing for the ordinary discharge of their duties, and also shoe leather. All classes under this Bill will be better off than they are now. The only class that has any occasion to complain is that which is now getting $600 and desires more pay, and which may not be satisfied with an increase of $26. We have a right to compare the salaries paid these men with those paid in other walks of life, to see whether these men are really underpaid at $600 a year. I suppose we would regard a street car conductor as a man sufficiently intelligent and qualified, physically, morally and mentally, to be a letter carrier. Well, the salary of an Ottawa street car conductor is $9 a week for ten hours work per day, whereas the pay of a letter carrier is $12 a week for an average day's labour of eight hours twenty-one minutes, or say nine hours. Or in a year the letter carrier gets $150 more than the man who is employed on an Ottawa street car. AVe do not need to take policemen or firemen or men of that class, but you can go into the big factories and look at the wages paid there. Take the tool makers in the machine shops, the lathers, the planers, the vice hands and fitters and others, and vou will find that they are not paid the wages paid in the Post Office Department. Is there any reason why a man who is a messenger

in the post office should have more wages than a man who has served an apprenticeship five, six or seven years in a manufacturing establishment V What are the necessary qualifications for a letter carrier? He requires sufficient intelligence and education to read the addresses on the letters and sufficient honesty to deliver them. He does not require any special training. AVhen I had the honour of appointing six letter carriers in Brantford, the system was arranged, the letters were delivered, and the whole thing worked like clock work from its very inception. There was not even a slip from the very start. That shows that it does not require special intelligence to do the work. We have got along so far without trouble or friction in Brantford. It may be said the letter carriers there do not do as much work as in Toronto and in Ottawa. But judging by the receipts in the Brantford post office, the Brantford postmen do more work than those of any other city in Canada, because the receipts are greater in proportion to the number of letter carriers than they are anywhere else in the Dominion. The work does not demand special intelligence. It does not require an apprenticeship of five or six years, and the wages of $600 per year are abnormally high as compared with those paid in other walks of life where years of apprenticeship are required and a considerable amount of technical skill. My sympathies are always witn the men who work for a daily wage, but at the same time we must not make the position of a letter carrier so exceedingly desirable that men in other avocations will begin to grumble. Why should a tool maker, a trade which requires superior expertness and years of experience, be paid less wages than a letter carrier ? A tool maker works in Toronto fifty-five hours for $14.70, and in Brantford fifty hours per week for $12. The lathe hand, who has to serve an apprenticeship of six years, gets in Brantford an average weekly wage of $9.25 for a day of twelve hours, and in Toronto $12 a week, which is a small wage compared with what is paid a post office messenger. And when these men only show up at 9 a.m., do they get paid a full day ? Not at all. And when they are absent one or two days on account of sickness, do they get paid in full ? No, they only get paid for the hours they work. In all these avocations a man is paid only the hours he labours, and I do not see why a letter carrier should be in a different position.
Take the planers and shapers in an engine shop, also high class work, they get from $10,30 to $11 per week in Brantford and $13 in Toronto. Take the vice hands and fitters, they get in Brantford from $10 to $11.80 per week and in Toronto $12.75. Then there are the drill hands, who do an inferior class of work, they only get $9 per week in Toronto. You can go through all the agricultural implement establishments in this
country, take any branch of their business requiring the greatest amount of training and years of apprenticeship, and no where are they paying the wages received by the letter carriers of Canada to-day. Go to St. Thomas, where recently the government built a drill shed under the schedule of fair wages, which is always regarded as pretty high, and what do we find. AVe find that the contractor's foreman carpenter gets $2.25 per day ; the excavators, $1.50 per day ; builders' labourers $1.50 per day ; joiners, $2 per day ; stair builders, $2 per day ; plumbers, $2 per day; metal roofers, $1.25 per day. I do not need to go on through the whole list, but when we find the highest class men in these factories are not paid as high a wage as $626 a year, we are justified in asking that their case be considered fairly on its merits and not solely from the point of view of its disadvantages. I am glad that in Brantford our letter carriers are pretty well satisfied with the arrangement now proposed. They drafted a resolution and sent it on to me as follows :
Dear Sir,-I am instructed by the letter carriers of Brantford to inform you that they have had a copy of the new Post Office Act, that is now before the House, and after giving it the consideration that is necessary to come to any conclusion as to its merits, and how it will affect us under present conditions, after all due consideration having been given to all the changes it contains, as far as it affects Brantford, we are satisfied with the Bill as it stands, and would ask you to support it in the House, as we are confident you will. We learn that Toronto is against it and may ask for its withdrawal, but we do not want to see any such thing happen, as we are of the opinion that or. the whole it is as good as the most of us could expect and better for us in Brantford than we expected, and we hope that it will become law without any opposition from the carriers.
On behalf of Brantford carriers, I have the honour to be,
Yours respectfully,
