That is the opinion of the men in Brantford, whose wages will be advanced immediately to the extent almost of $146 per annum. Why should they not approve of this ? There is not a man in the whole employ of the Post Office Department, there is not a letter carrier who has any right to complain except the man who is now getting $600 a year, and will only get $26 more. I have stated that a wage of $2 a day for a man who gets his appointment, say at the age of 25 and holds it as long as he can do the work has a pretty good thing. Take the agricultural implement shops, the Massey-Harris Company. They will pay their hands a less wage than these letter carriers get. and for ten weeks in the year they are shut down.
There is hardly an agricultural implement shop in this country in which they do not lay off their men from six to ten weeks in the year, and they do not then pay as high

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: a rate of wages as is paid to these men. Take bricklayers, earning $3 a day ; they apparently get big wages, but they only work for eight months in the year. Plasterers earn $3 a day, but work nine months in the year. Stonemasons are paid $3 a day and work for only nine months in the year. And all these trades require skill, they require training, they require an apprenticeship. These employees of the country get more money than those engaged in other avocations, and besides they have steady employment, no dockages as long as they discharge their duties, and they have the possibility before them of getting Into a class in which they will draw $700 a year. They have no right to complain. The Postmaster General in this Bill, is treating the employees of the country with almost prodigal liberality, such as I am fully persuaded, will satisfy the great mass of the letter carriers.

I think the bon. gentleman's (Mr. Heyd's) defence of the Bill is commendable from his point of view, and admirably gotten up. But it is not quite so strong as it might appear to be. The hon. gentleman evidently starts with the assumption that any one who rises to ask a question is thereby condemning the Bill.
I did not say that.

That is the .only inference to be drawn from the tenor of the hon. gentleman's argument. And the Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Mulock) when invited to give legitimate information which might enable us to judge the merits of the Bill seems to jump at the same conclusion. My first observation with regard to the Bill was designed to elicit on this point-it seemed that the effect of the Bill would be to remove a large class of civil servants from under the provisions of the Civil Service Act, and I wished to know in what respect that law was defective. It seemed to me that, if the Civil Service Act were not what it should be, it would be better to prepare one that was more suitable and so improve the whole service, rather thap make a special law for one class. I regret that the asking of questions with a view to gaining reasonable information disturbs the Postmaster General and rutiles his temper. When members put courteous questions, I think they are entitled to respectful answers, without the minister immediately concerned jumping to the conclusion that the request for information indicates opposition to his proposals. I had neither intention nor desire to oppose the Bill, but merely sought to elicit such information as would enable me to judge whether this Bill would improve the public service and do greater justice to public officers than the Civil Service Act or not. I do not think that any member of parliament is stepping aside from his duty in asking for such questions, and I think that a Minister of the Crown is doing 1 Mr. HEYD.
less than his duty who is not prepared to answer those questions courteously. The time when the Bill is brought up is the time for us to get information that we may intelligently judge of the merits of the Bill. The hon. Postmaster General, no doubt, gave us a great deal of information in connection with the measure. But there was information he did not give, whether it was because he misunderstood the question or because his mind was running in another channel and he wished to engage in a general defence of the Bill, I do not know. At any rate, he seemed to be more anxious to prove that the Bill would have good results and that it would do justice to the letter carriers than to compare the Bill with the Civil Service Act and prove that this Bill is better. I listened with a good deal of attention to the speech in support of the Bill delivered by the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd). I have no doubt the hon. gentleman prepared his brief very carefully. When he read his certificate of character to the Bill which he had received from the letter carriers, it sounded to me as if it were something prepared by the hon. gentleman himself to give to the House as a clincher of his argument.
If I may be permitted. I would like to say that I did not know the letter carriers had had a meeting and passed resolutions or that they were going to write to me.

I am glad to know that, because it relieves my mind of the impression that the whole thing had been got up by the hon. gentleman himself and that he had done it out of kindness to the Postmaster General and to help him over a difficult place. It seems necessary that I should assure the Postmaster General that I am not opposing the Bill, nor do I regard the Bill as altogether a bad one. I think it has some features that might be improved, but that in some respects it is ahead of the Civil Service Act. But there is one thing about it that struck me from the first as being somewhat inappropriate. If the Civil Service Act is not a suitable one, it seems to me we ought to amend it and have all branches of the service under the one Act.
There are many others besides the letter carriers who are outside the Act.

I know there are. And for that reason I have always regarded the Civil Service Act as requiring amendment. If the Civil Service Act is entirely unsuitable, we ought to do away with it and have another in its place. I would not complain of this Bill if it results in giving us more efficient employees and in doing justice to those wffio engaged in the service of the country. But I wish the Postmaster General to understand that when I put a question I do not put it with a desire of in-

terfering with him in the discharge of his duties, or of ruffling his usually good temper in conducting matters on the floor of the House.

I would like to ask the Postmaster General if he does not think that this would be a good time to provide for a free delivery system in all the cities of the; Dominion ? I notice that some cities have that system, while others of equal importance are without it. That strikes one as not being in accord with the principle of one law for all. My hon. friend from Brantford was able to tell us how well things were working in Brantford and how the Bill would apply there. I can hardly know anything about the matter because we have no letter carriers. Yet I represent as important a city as does the hon. gentleman, the city of St. Catharines. As we have no free delivery system there I can hardly know what these hon. gentlemen are talking about. Would not this be a good time for the Postmaster General to propose an enactment, if an enactment is necessary, that all cities of the Dominion shall have the same system of free delivery ? Of course I can understand that in large cities there must be more frequent delivery than in small cities. In a city like Toronto they may well require five or six deliveries a day. But why should not a city like St. Catharines have at least two deliveries, one in the morning and one in the afternoon. What fairness is there to that part of the country in the present state of affairs ? I would like to ask the Postmaster General to give me some words of encouragement as to what we may look for in that respect.

When I took charge of the department I found that St. Catharines was not enjoying free delivery. The hon. gentleman's friends had had an opportunity during many years of giving that city a free delivery system.
The city has grown since then.

I am glad to hear it has made such progress, and I hope the government have contributed toward it. I have made some progress in the way of extending the free delivery system by giving it to the city of Brantford. Therefore, my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) will see that there is movement in the direction he suggests. I am not able to tell him, however, on what day the system will take effect in St. Catharines. Such a provision will not find an appropriate place in a Bill of this kind, an item in the estimates would be necessary for that purpose. Whenever Council can be induced to provide the ways and means, then the Post Office Department will put the system into force.

I was glad to hear the hon. member for Grey declare that he was heartily in sympathy with this Bill. I may
say that I also rejoice that this Bill has been introduced, because I do not think there is the slightest doubt but that it is a great improvement on anything that we have had, so far as letter carriers are concerned. We have quite a staff in the city of Vancouver, somewhere over thirty now, which this Bill more or less affects, and I think I voice their sentiment in saying that they will be very glad of the changes proposed in this Bill. So far as I have information by letter, they are very anxious, in common with other letter carriers of the Dominion, that some change should be made for their benefit. While they have naturally been looking for more, perhaps, than they are going to get, I think every fair-minded man will come to the conclusion that they are on the whole fairly treated in the present Bill. The hon. member for Brantford might have gone a good deal further in his remarks, so far as the pay of the men is concerned in his province. I have in mind a class of men who have to spend three or four years at a university in the Dominion of Canada, and then have to take a theological training as well, and the salary of the great bulk of that profession in Canada to-day is from $600 to $700 a year. So that when we compare their salary with that of the letter carriers, I think the latter receive very fail treatment, not only from the government, but from the people of Canada. But my main object in rising was to say a word in favour of the stampers and sorters of the post office.

They are affected In the
same way.

No, they are not included in the Bill, and I would like to have them included. So far as Vancouver is concerned, we have some very intelligent and industrious young men who have been appointed as stampers and sorters, and who show considerable intelligence by the fact that they have passed the qualifying examination. Their pay is particularly small I think for men of that calibre.
What do they receive
$40 a month, the same as the letter carriers. I think the benefits are so important in this Bill that they ought to be extended to the stampers and sorters.

I would suggest to the minister that he add a clause to his Bill giving all cities of 10,000 inhabitants the benefit of free mail delivery. I think that would meet the approbation of nearly all cities of that size in Canada.

There are some good features in this Bill, and I cheerfully recognize that fact. I refer to the shortening of the time, after a man enters the service as a letter carrier, when he may receive the maximum salary of the position. I think in view of the fact that the Post-

master General has abolished the Superannuation Act he was in duty bound to shorten the time, and I congratulate him upon having done so. A young man who is qualified to act as letter carrier does not require to train for six, eight or nine years before he receives the maximum salary. If he is not fit to discharge the duties of letter carrier at the end of two or three years, he ought not to be permitted to remain in the service. I think it is only reasonable and just that the amendment which the Postmaster General has made should receive the approval of the House. I cordially support it, and have great pleasure in doing so. But when the >hon. gentleman and his friends opposite attempt to argue that this Bill improves the position of the letter carriers of this country beyond what it was before he came into office, he has a very difficult proposition to prove. He and his friends seem to forget that before the Superannuation Act was abolished the letter carriers contributed 2 per cent of their salary towards a superannuation fund, and after they had served from 20 to 35 years they got a pension of 20-50ths or 35-50ths as the case might be, of their salary for the remainder of their lives. The abolition of that Act put this class of men who have been appoiuted since that time, upon a very different footing from that occupied by the carriers .before. The position of a carrier under the Superannuation Act was far better than it is under the proposed amendment to the law. I need not take up. the time elaborating that fact, it must be patent to every one who will give it consideration. But I refer particularly to the case of men who entered the service prior to 1896, the men who have served the public as letter carriers for a great many years, and it must not be forgotten that these men served the country on a very small salary for a number of years, commencing at $300 ' and increasing by $30 a year ; but, as the hon. gentleman says, it took eight or nine years to attain the maximum of their class. These men are not benefited by this Act; and these men constitute the vast majority of the letter carriers of this Dominion. Their position is not improved in any way by the Act which has been introduced, notwithstanding the fact that they have been very largely supported by public sentiment in the demands which they have made for several years past upon the Post Office Department for an increase. Now, it seems to me they have not been treated as frankly as they had a right to expect, in view ofthe statements that were made to them when a deputation waited upon the Postmaster General .to represent and to advocate their case. During his absence last year the question of remuneration to be paid to letter carriers was brought before the House by the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Birkett). I find in the ' Hansard ' of May 21, last year, at page 5792, the following remarks by the hon. member for Ottawa :
Where is the member for Nanaimo ?

I do not know where the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Smith) is. He is not in his seat. I have no doubt he is otherwise engaged. During the early part of the year the * Globe ' newspaper took up the cudgels on behalf of the letter carriers and strongly supported their contention for an increase of pay. I find, on January 6th, the following article:-
The Letter Carriers' Pay.
The Post Office Department ought to begin the new year by raising the salaries of the letter carriers. Rent, food and expenses of all kinds are higher to-day than some years ago, and the carriers' wages are now altogether too low. Economy is a good thing, no doubt, but what, can be done by keeping down the wages of tbesie men will make hardly an appreciable difference in the annual expenditure of the Dominion, while it makes a big difference to the postmen. Parliament ought to sympathize with these mien. The Indemnity of members of parliament, including the senators, has been raised from $1,000 to $1,500. If it costs a member $1,500 to live for four months, how does he expect a postman to live for a year on a fifth or fourth of that amount ? This matter has now been delayed long enough, and we hope that the very reasonable request of these faithful servants ol' the public will be complied with at an early clay.
The hon. Postmaster General, in the statement which he presented to the House, gave statistics as to the pay which was given to the letter carriers as far back as 25 or 30 years ago, but it is an acknowledged fact, and the hon. gentleman will not deny
it, that the cost of living has substantially increased since that time. The letter carriers, living in cities, have to pay more rent, they have to pay more for their food than they did then, and in view of the increased expenditures which they are called upon to make in order to live it is not unreasonable or unfair that the demand which they have made should receive the favourable consideration of the government. The hon. Postmaster General has the advantage of having at his elbow all the time the Minister of Labour to aid in preparing measures affecting the working classes, and I am sure that hon. gentleman must have drawn his attention to the resolutions which have been passed by representative labour organizations as to the compensation which the letter carriers are receiving to-day. On page 33 of the report of the Proceedings of the Eighth Annual Session of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, held at Toronto, September 8th-14th, 1892. the following resolution was adopted. This resolutipn was moved by the gentleman who now occupies the position of fair-wage officer in the Department of Labour, and it was seconded by the gentleman who now occupies the position of secretary of the Labour Bureau of the province of Ontario. These gentlemen were well qualified apparently to speak in the interests of those on whose beihalf the resolution was moved. The congress which they addressed was so impressed with the reasonableness of the resolution that it was passed unanimously. I will read it for the information of the committee :
Moved by Mr. D. J. O'Donohue, seconded by Mr. R. Glockling and resolved,
That in the opinion of this congress the minimum salary of letter carriers in the public service should be not less than $600 per annum, and that it be an instruction to the executive committee of this congress to use Its best efic.rts In pressing this view of the case upon the government.
In 1898 the Trades and Labour Congress wrestled with the subject again and passed the following resolution :-
Moved by Mr. Mortimer, seconded by Mr. Watson and resolved,
Whereas, the letter carriers and other postal assistants of Canada have frequently appeared before different trades councils of the Dominion and complained that the conditions under which they worked were not such as should exist among government employees ; and whereas, these trade councils have investigated and found that these men had a just grievance, in that they received insufficient wages, had no set hours of labour and had no definite system of promotion ; therefore be It resolved, that we urge upon the Dominion government the necessity of establishing a minimum wage of $2 a day for eight hours work, and so regulating the department chat letter carriers may depend upon promotion for faithful services.
Last year, at Brantford, the Trades and Labour Congress again dealt with this matter, so that the attention of the hon. Postmaster General and his colleagues must

have been drawn to the attitude which organized labour has taken in respect to the pay of the letter carriers. In 1901 this resolution was adopted :
That the letter carriers of the Dominion having, by petition, requested the hon. Postmaster General to consider the advisability and justice of granting an increase of 20 per cent in the present scale of wages, and gs the letter carriers have not as yet received the consideration which their petition merited, be it
Resolved, that it be an instruction to the incoming executive committee of this congress to i.rimediately, by petition or otherwise, draw the serious attention of the Postmaster General to the fact that the increased prices of the various necessaries of lit3, such as food, rent and fuel, render it necessary that this urgent and important question should receive immediate and favourable consideration and settlement.
Now, Mr. Chairman, what consideration has been given in this Bill to the large body of the letter carriers of the Dominion ? Has their position been improved ? Not in the slightest degree. Those who have been in the service for eight years and have obtained the maximum are getting $49 per month, while in the scale provided for by the Postmaster General those in class D will receive $49.40. That is the only difference I can see, except that in the case of men appointed since 1896, they may reach the maximum in 44 years, hut, as I have said, those who have already obtained the maximum pay will not have their position improved in the slightest degree. They have asked for bread and it looks to me as if they had received from the Postmaster General a stone. Their position remains exactly as it was before. There is not the slightest difference made in their position, notwithstanding the petitions which they have presented from time to time ; notwithstanding the assurances which they have received from the Postmaster General and his colleagues; notwithstanding that they have established that the cost of living has substantially increased during the past five years. The position of these letter carriers, proven to have been unsatisfactory, has not been bettered in the slightest by the Bill introduced by the minister (Hon. Mr. Mulock). It does not affect the men who are receiving the maximum. The hon. gentleman from Brantford (Mr. Heyd) read a resolution that was passed by the letter carriers of his city. Their position undoubtedly will be improved under the operation of the Bill, and they ought to give credit to the Postmaster General. But the reason why their position will he improved is because they have only been appointed during the last two or three years, and they will reach the maximum in a shorter time than if the provisions of the old Act were in force. They are in duty bound to give credit to the Postmaster General, because the Bill beneficially affects them to that extent. I do not desire to speak at

greater length, because I know that the time of the minister is very short here this afternoon, and I would not like to interfere in any way with his arrangements. I repeat that the Postmaster General has not done what the letter carriers expected he would do, or what they were given to understand he would do. No amount of specious argument can establish that the position of these industrious, hard working, faithful men has been improved in any way by this measure. In August last there was a flourish of trumpets in the ' Evening Star,' a very excellent paper printed in Toronto, which supports the Postmaster General, and it was owing to the fact that somevorder had been issued by the Post Office Department respecting the purchase of supplies for use in that department. It is worth reading. It says:
Current Wages and Union Hours-The stipulations for all who furnish Post Office supplies.
Ottawa, Aug. 28.-Hon. William Mulock has decided that all men or firms furnishing supplies of all kinds to the Post Office' Department must pay the current rate of wages to their employees and adopt the union hours of labour. This applies to goods whether, sold under contract or not. At present the regulations apply only to contracts, but the principle has now been extended so as to become operative in thie case of all who are on the patronage list of the department. Hereafter all persons who sell goods to the Post. Office Department will have to make a sworn declaration that they have complied with the new regulation before they will receive payment.
If that statement is correcc, the Postmaster General deserves credit for having issued the regulation, but I think the rule should apply to the employees in his own department as well as to those from whom supplies are purchased. It is a notorious fact that those who have been employed in his department in collecting letters from the street letter boxes have had to work seven nights in the week. Their hours of labour are more than nine or ten hours. They were on duty from eight o'clock in the morning until sometimes ten o'clock or eleven o'clock at night. I think, therefore, that it is a good rule to have a regulation of this kind apply first of ail to the employees of the hon. gentleman's own department. 1 think charity, justice, and fair play should commence at home, and I believe with my hon. friend from Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) that an amendment should be made in this Bill, fixing the hours which the letter carriers have to work, if their wages are not to be increased. The hon. gentleman said that one man could distribute a greater number of letters -in a given time than another. That is quite true, but I wish to say that so far as the city of Toronto is concerned, in many cases the letter carriers are overburdened with work. They are not able to carry out all the letters and mail matter, and so not only automobiles but

wagons are used to bring an additional load to meet them on their beats, when they have their work partially done. This is a condition that should be remedied. These men are employed, some of them, from six o'clock and half past six in the morning until five and half past five at night, and they are out in the most severe weather. As the hon. gentleman knows, they are employed on holidays, when there is at least one delivery. They have to discharge arduous duties; they are a faithful body of men, and they deserve better consideration from the Postmaster General. I hope that before this Bill goes through, the Postmaster General will concede that the grades shall be rearranged, and that men, after having served a reasonable time in class D, will be put into class E. There is no provision made for them going into class E, except on the recommendation of the officer who has supervision. The whole trend of this Act places these employees practically in the hands of the administration of the day. They need not be raised from class A to class B, or from class B to class C, or from class C to class D, or raised to class E unless the officer says so. The letter-carriers who are affected by this Bill are entirely in the hands of the government of the day; they will owe their promotion to superior officers in every case, and in that way the Bill will have an injurious effect, and ought to be amended before it is passed. I would suggest that it should be amended in this way:	That unless these men are
reported against as being inefficient, they should in the natural order of things and at the end of a given time be promoted from class to class. Is that an unreasonable proposition? I submit that promotion should not be ou account of some extraordinarily arduous service, but that if they have faithfully served for a given number of years they should be promoted from class D to class E. Why is grade E put in ? Why is the hope held out that they may some day succeed in getting $2.25 a day? Who is to determine when that promotion is to be accorded to them ? It is most unfair to them that the provision should be worded in that way. The highest class ought to be attainable by them after a reasonable length of service with good conduct, or else it ought to be struck out of the Bill altogether. I hope the minister will amend clause 3 by providing that at the end of a certain number of years men shall be promoted from grade D to grade E, thus making the maximum $2.25 per day, instead of $2 as at present. The men who are now in the service get holidays and they are paid if they are absent on sick leave. Under the provisions of this Bill they get 14 days holidays, but they have now 21 days, and under the Bill they will receive no pay whatever if they are sick. Is their position improved under the new order of things? Not at all. The Postmaster General says 128
that if men are not paid for the time they are absent on account of sickness there will be less sickness. That is hardly a warranted reflection to make on these men. If men are found shirking their work; if men are found shamming sickness they should be dismissed from the service. I repeat that the position accorded to the letter carriers under this Bill is a much less favourable one than the letter carriers of the Dominion had a right to expect. I hope that the Postmaster General will so amend the Bill, that after a certain number of years' service men can reach class E and receive $2.25 a day, and that some definite time should be fixed as to the number of hours in a day's work. The hon. member for Winnipeg says the day should be eight hours. That is a reasonable proposition, and I hope it will be embodied in the Bill before it is eventually passed.
I notice that in the United States Congress an effort is being made to substantially increase the pay of the letter carriers on the other side, and the same arguments are there used on behalf of the men as may fairly be used here. For instance, the increased cost of living and the increased amount of work done. Under these circumstances and in view of the efficient manner in which our carriers do their work, I think the Postmaster General1 pught to make the maximum pay at least $2.25 per day, and fix the hours of labour at not more than eight in the eleven. If the Bill were amended in these respects, I am sure it would be generally acceptable to all the men in the service and be highly appreciated.
I notice that there is a clause providing for the appointment of a superintendent of the city post offices. Who is superintending the city post offices now ? Is the work not being done efficiently now ?

There is no regular provision for the superintending of city post offices in the full sense of the word. These offices are supposed to be more or less under the supervision of the inspector, but the post office inspectors have not got that intimate acquaintance with the technical post office work which makes them competent to discharge the duties that would be required of a chief city superintendent. I mentioned on a former occasion the gentleman I had in my mind for the office, and I think my hon. friend will agree that a better appointment could not be made.

I find that one of the objections in the minds of the letter carriers is this. Under the present Civil Service Act, the wages of the letter carriers, sorters, and others increase from $360 to $600 per year by annual increases of $30. The letter carriers are under the impression that this works automatically, and that the increase takes place without the intervention of anybody, but under the new Bill, a recommen-



dation is required and thus the increase may be refused.

I may say that parliament was informed some time ago that the late Minister of Justice, Sir Oliver Mowat, gave it as his legal opinion that no civil servant was entitled to the annual increase provided in the Civil Service Act, except on the recommendation of the Governor General in Council, and on the money being voted by parliament. He gave it as his opinion that no civil servant has any legal right to the increase, but that the*, increase is a matter wholly within the discretion of parliament and the government. Recommendations for the increases are therefore necessary to-day, and these words do not in the slightest degree vary the law, but give expression to what is the law, so that the letter caiTiers and others will know quite well that they have to depend for their increase upon the recommendation for the promotion. There is every disposition to be lenient with all public officers. In my own department my instructions are that every civil servant, who has a salary of $800 or less, should be given the annual increment unless there is good ground for disqualifying him. Every one is given the increase unless his superior officer reports against him. That is the rule adopted, and it is no unkindness to the staff to let them understand that even if the hand is not very often used, there is a master hand which may be used. They are treated with the utmost consideration, and this Bill is in no sense a measure to give arbitrary power, which might or might not be abused, and I am satisfied that these observations which I am making will be of benefit to the staff themselves. They are meant In kindness, whether accepted in that light or not. As to the provisions whereby some of the letter carriers might be promoted to class E at $2.25 per day, there will be some appointments of that kind, especially in the leading cities, where there are greater responsibilities devolving upon some of the letter carriers and where their duties are perhaps more onerous. Those who are getting the maximum to-day will get $26 more to begin with, and if they work the 313 days they Will get a $20 bonus besides, if their services were satisfactory. It is not meant that the work must be specially satisfactory, but what would be considered a reasonably fair and satisfactory service, such as would commend itself to any respectable man. Public officers cannot withhold or give certificates arbitrarily. They are amenable to public opinion even if they are not actuated by conscientious motives, and the general disposition is to be very friendly to those beneath them. You can rely on it that every superior officer will, wherever possible, recommend the letter carriers and these other various officials for the increase, and unless these officials have disqualified themselves

by bad conduct, they will get the extra $20 as well as the $26. Those in receipt of $600 a year will get $46 extra, and will have the chance of getting a further increase in grade E of $78 a year. The increase of $46 on the salary of $600 is an increase of between 7 per cent and 8 per cent, which is not an insignificant increase.
As regards the hon. gentleman's statement that I had made some promise, I must disclaim anything of the kind. I am aware that some organizations have passed resolutions in which I am reported as having promised to a delegation which waited on me in March, 1901, that there would be an increase. But I was extremely careful, as I am on all occasions, not to make any promise. You have yet to find an occasion when I have made a promise to any individual or deputation as to what the government or council would do. What I stated was that the matter would receive my best consideration, and that I hoped to mature a plan which I would leave with my hon. colleague the Minister of Finance to present to parliament. The Minister of Finance was present. I had a scheme in my mind at the time, which is somewhat the same as that presented to-day, and which does provide a measure of Increase to those who chose to avail themselves of it. I wrote a confidential report to my colleague, the Minister of Finance, setting forth my views and requesting him to take up the measure and bring it before my colleagues. But during my voyage I came to the conclusion that the views that I had left behind were not sufficiently definite and that it would be better to defer the matter until the present session, and I cabled to my colleague, the Minister of Finance, to that effect. But I want to make it quite clear that I never made a promise beyond what I have stated on the floor of the House to-day.
I understand that there is a rule in force that no man can be appointed as a letter carrier who is over 25 years of age. Will that be rescinded by the adoption of this Bill ?

Yes. There are many persons over 25 years of age who would be able to perform the duties of these various positions, such as packers, messengers, and so on ; and if they are paid by the day, there is not the same objection to men advanced in years being appointed that there would be if they were paid by the year.
The Postmaster General said, if I understood him correctly, that all the persons affected by this Bill would receive at least $46 a year increase.
Yes.

If I read section 7 correctly. I do not so interpret it. Probably the Postmaster General can set me right.

The men now receiving the maximum will not come under section 7, will they ?
If they wish.
But they will have to abandon their superannuation ?
No, there is a saving clause in section 0, which provides that they shall not.

I hope the Postmaster General will extend the privileges of class ' E ' to the present employees, whether they accept the provisions of this Bill or not. There is a strong feeling among the old employees of the department that this Bill does not do them justice. The hon. minister has told us, as the fact is, that the present employees to attain the maximum salary have to serve nine or ten years. There are many who have served these lime or ten years, and there are a good many I ernaps who have served six or seven years. By this Bill these men will have placed side by side with them other men who will attain the maximum salary in four and a half years. That will, I think, breed discontent and a state of things not to the advantage of the service. If the men now in the service were allowed to have the advantages of class ' E ' in common with those who come under the Bill, I think it would do much to remove any cause of dissatisfaction in that rewpeei. I think it is not a gracious tiling foi the government to tr;a. an old and faithful civil servant in such a way that he has to be coerced to accept this Bill in order to get the advantage of it. It does seem reasonable that the special class ' E ' should not lie confined to men who ire appointed after this date, but should ais be open to old servants who have served the public well in the past.

lias the hon. Postmaster General considered the suggestion made by the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. .Maxwell), to include sorters and stampers in clause 1 ?
The POSTMASTER GENERAL When we get through the Bill. I propose to offer an amendment in the form of an independent substantive clause dealing with stamp-eis and sorters.

Will you allow me to make another appeal ? According to the ruling of the Postmaster General a short time ago. the age limit at which a man could enter the service was changed. He must now be between 18 and 25, and I am in hearty sympathy with that rule. I think the younger you can get a man into the service the better, both for the service and for himself. But unfortunately there were a number of men in the service before that rule came into force, and these men, after having passed-some the pre-128J
limiuary and others the qualifying examination-were refused to be put on the permanent list because of the age limit. When this Bill is coming into force, I think it would lie a gracious act to allow all those men who have been in the post office service to receive the benefit of the Act as well as the permanent staff.

I think my hon. friend's request is perfectly reasonable, and I will say that it is intended, as soon as this measure becomes law, to go through the list of all those now performing temporary work, and all who are suit-aide to be brought under the provisions of this Bill will be brought under its provisions.
On section 3,

This provides that those in grade 'A' shall receive only $1.25 per day. Even the trackmen ou the Intercolonial Railway are going to be paid above that rate very soon, and it seems to me that this is too low a sum to recognize here as a minimum at all. Seeing that the grade only lasts six months, I think it would be a great deal bettter to make this read that the salaries of those in grades ' A ' and ' B ' shall be at the rate of $1.50 per day. The hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) says that in this class of work a man is efficient as soon as he enters the service. There is nothing to learn; there is no apprenticeship; it is work that needs a man and not a boy; and therefore there is no reason why he should be paid at that low rate. It seems to me that it should be fixed at $1.50. Then a man would be in grade ' A ' while on probation, and when it was decided to appoint him permanently, he would be moved into grade ' B.'

I am willing to meet my hon. friend's objection in a certain way. The six months is about as short a probationary period as you could reasonably fix; but if a man deserves the appointment sooner, then the $1.50 will begin. I am willing to put in words to provide that he shall be subject to a probationary period of not less than six months, or until he shall on the recommendation of the proper officer, be sooner confirmed in his appointment.
That goes a long way towards meeting the point. But if I were the Postmaster General and were willing to go that far, I would do away with this eyesore of $1.25 a day.

No, 1 want efficiency.

I would like to know if there is any possibility of this grade ' E ' being made more open. I suppose that the idea "at present is that very few will enter it. But it seems to me that any man who has not been especially reported against ought, after twelve years service, to enter grade ' E ' as a matter of right.

I think it better to let the Bill go into force as it is in that respect. We will see how it works for a while. I could not agree to-day to any amendment.
Subsection, as amended, agreed to.
On section 4, subsection 2,

I think the Postmaster General will see the reasonableness of asking that that subsection be altered in some way. It seems to me that the principle of reduction in grade as a man grows older should not be recognized.
It is the law to-day.

It should be worded in some way so that, in the interest of discipline a man may be subject to suspension from time to time. But, for myself, I totally object to the subsection in its present form, because it involves what seems to me an altogether harmful principle. This power to reduce the officers in grade may not be used except in case of change of government. or something like that, but the subsection does give the department power as a man grows older to reduce him in grade.

But it does not change the law. Civil servants are liable to be reduced in grade at any time. That is very rarely done, but it is quite right that they should understand that it is possible. Civil servants are sometimes reduced in rank.
Is it to be done by Order in Council ?
Of course.
Would it not be better to say so here ?
That is covered by section 12. which provides that appointments, promotions, reductions in grade and dismissals under this Act shall be made by the Governor in Council.

Then, why put in this subsection at all ? If it is put in it must be because it is expected that it will be made use of. The idea is to reduce men as they grow inefficient. And, of course, when it is a matter of carrying weight and walking

This is a clause that is in the interest of the employees, for it makes it possible to continue old men in the service. According to my hon. friend's (Mr. Puttee's) view the employees should be kept so long as they can work under the full head of steam, and then dismiss them. But, under this subsection that will not be necessary, but a man can be given suitable work as his efficiency grows less. Whether it works well or otherwise depends upon the man in whose hands it is. An arbitrary use can be made of any power, or a fair use can be made of it. Governments are amenable to public opinion, and I do not thinly it would be fair to assume that this power will be cruelly or unfairly used. The same power exists with regard to the whole civil service to-day, and it is as well for those in the whole service to be aware of the existence of this power.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What are these sections that are repealed ?

The only change in this section is this :	There
is at present a fund derived from assessments to make good losses that arise through the default or wrong-doing of any of our officers, and it has been held that we cannot use that fund for payment to any one except to the Crown. For example, a person has deposited money in our savings bank, and suppose a postmaster has embezzled that money, we could draw upon the assessment in respect to that loss. But if an individual transmitted a letter containing money througn the post office and one of our officers misappropriated it, although it was quite clear who had done it, we could not pay out of the assessment to the individual who had lost the money. The amendment is to make that fund liable to the individual citizen in case of a loss sustained toy him.

speechtext: How do these regulations come before parliament, or do they come before parliament in any way? How does parliament know what they are V

They have to be gazetted, and they are published in the Post Office Guide, and they get to the public in that way. I do not know that there is any other way of their receiving publicity. Would the hon. gentleman (Mr Borden, Halifax) suggest something ?

We generally incorporate them wherever we can. \ve want to give them the widest publicity. Still, I will endeavour to meet the hon. gentleman's suggestion as far as I can.
On section 13,

This is really an amendment which is not necessary. It is quite impossible to fix the exact length of time that a letter carrier will be on his beat. He must remain on his beat until his work is completed. If the hon. gentleman would peruse the time tables in Canada I am sure he would not make that suggestion, because he will find that in many instances the length of service is under eight hours. We cannot measure oft the beats so as to fix the exact time during which a man will be out. When he goes out upon his beat he must stay there until the work is completed. The average number of hours during which letter carriers work throughout the whole of Canada is eight hours and twenty-one minutes.

The work is being steadily increased, and of course it takes longer to do it. The number of letters to be delivered on each man's beat is steadily increasing. He has to go up and down stairs and up and down in elevators, and all that kind of thing, and it might not be unreasonable to expect that you should fix some hour for commencing and finishing work.

The debate is sufficient to indicate the view of the committee, and we will endeavour to live up to the spirit of the discussion this afternoon. The practice in the past has not inflicted any serious injustice on these men, and you can depend upon it that we will not retrograde at least. I propose to move an amendment to the Bill. There is at present a third class jn the post office outside service entering at $400 and going

up to $800. I propose to divide that third class into two classes, one to be called the fourth class, which will come in at $400 and go up to $000, and the other to begin at $600 and go up to $800, to take power to transfer to that third class stampers and sorters, and to make the annual increment in the case' of the fourth class $50 a year. LaRIVIERE (Provencher). Mr. Speaker, I am not going to offer any factious opposition t* this Bill ; hut there seems to he a fatality attached to it. I see that the French translation of the Bill provides for the incorporation of the church, not the bishop, while in the English version it is the bishop of the Orthodox Greek Church. I must also call the attention of the House to the fact that in the body of the Bill there is no responsible name at all. We are asked to incorporate the bishop of the Orthodox Russo-Greek Catholic Church of North America and the Aleutian Islands and his successors in office. A bishop has no successor in office as bishop, because the word bishop itself does not imply that there is a succession.

How do you know ?
Mr. LaRIVIERE. How do I know that a king never dies ? We had a Bill before a committee this morning, containing the name of a bishop, and we incorporated that bishop and his successors in office. Surely we ought to have a responsible name, because a bishop in that sense is not an individual. There are many other irregularities in connection with this Bill. The party who is seeking incorporation under this title has never proved his identity. We have no petition besides his own, and, as I said on another occasion, he is a foreigner living in a foreign country. Before recognizing the authority of that high clerical official, I think the House should give this matter a second thought. speechtext: The hon. gentleman promised to bring down the stub check-book showing the checks that were paid during January and February to the friends up in Lisgar.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: H.as the hon. gentleman laid any information on the Table with regard to a matter which I brought to his attention ? I asked him to give me the names of the enumerators who had their attention directed to the charges of fraud iu connection with the taking of the census, before these charges were made public.

I may say to the hon. gentleman that I was misinformed when I said I believed that the enumerators had been notified of the charges made against them. I believe there was only one enumerator really who was spoken to about this investigation, and he .was spoken to informally by the hon. member for Bag*t, wiho was looking into the matter in the county of Bagot. I had a conversation with Mr. O'Connor, of Montreal, who made the investigation there. He told me that one of the enumerators, who had been working in 1891, was enumerator also in his division In 1901. I asked him if he had spoken to this enumerator, and he said that he had not spoken to him definitely, although he had asked him about it, but intended doing so. I thought he had done so, but I fotmd afterwards that he had not. I thought that several other gentlemen were spoken to, but I find that they were not.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. gentleman was very positive the other day that a number of the enumerators had these charges of fraud brought to their attention, and had been requested to send in their replies before those charges were made public. The hon. gentleman ought to know positively before making any statement of the kind. I think it is one of the most humiliating admissions ever made by any man in this House, which the Minister of Agriculture has just made. He admits that he has brought charges broadcast against these men, and that in not one instance were these charges! brought to their attention before they were made. What justification has the hon. gentleman for slandering these men behind their backs and scattering those charges throughout the length and breadth of the country, without giving them the opportunity of saying a word in their defence ? It is only due to the hon. gentleman himself and the government and this House that some justification of that extraordinary mode of procedure should be given. We have these charges made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and then repeated over and over again by the hon. gentleman. I did not think it possible that such a course could have been adopted without some notice having been given these men. The charges against them were not made under oath. These enumerators were not given the opportunity of examining witnesses, but they were denounced as guilty of fraud on these ex parte statements, not made under oath, and made against men who were under oath in the discharge of their duties. Surely there must be some explanation of this extraordinary mode of procedure. Surely it has not been resorted to merely to make political capital.

What we wanted was to get at the proof and find out what explanation there was of the extraordinary condition of affairs, shown by comparisons of the figures of the census of 1891 with those of 1901. The figures of 1901 showed in many cases great decreases in population, in places where the people, who were familiar with the neighbourhood, could not believe such decreases could have taken place. The first mode of procedure was to try and check over the results of the census of 1901, and in the province of Quebec we had a ready means in the paroeliial returns of making this check. Our chock shows that the census of 1901 was fairly accurate. The difference between the parochial, and the census returns of 1901, in twenty-one constituencies, was only 8,000, and that was as close as could be expected, considering the three months difference in time between the two. The question then was whether there had been any mistake in the census returns of 1891. Going back we found a difference of 44,000 between the census of 1891 and the parochial returns of that year, which was a most extraordinary discrepancy. The question then was: Where did this discrepancy take place ? We found that a number of people had been enumerated in the Dominion census, who were not present when that census was taken, and we established this by incontrovertible evidence. I must confess that while I expected that some of the enumerators implicated had been notified, I did not give any definite instructions to that effect, and did not take any particular means for the purpose of consulting them. The evidence we had was such that it was impossible not to believe that the enumerators had unduly swelled the returns of 1891, and that being the case, I could not see any necessity for consulting the enumerators. No doubt if I had, they would have tried to shuffle out of the responsibility.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is certainly a remarkable reason. The hon. gentle-1 man listens to ex parte statements, not made

40S0
under oath, made behind the backs of these men, and assumes them to be true. He says that these men are such scoundrels that there is no use at all appealing to them. Just as if some one should accuse the kon. gentleman of burglarly, and a third person should be appealed to who would say that the hon. gentleman was guilty. It would be suggested that the bon. gentleman should be heard in his own defence, but the answer would be :	No, if the Hon. Sydney Fisher
is guilty of burglarly there is no- use in asking him, because he would deny it. That is a specimen of the hon. gentleman's logic with regard to these men. And he considers that lie is doing justice to himself, I suppose, when he makes .that explanation. He accused these men over and over again, in his speech, of fraud, and this is the only answer that he has to give to this House and to tlie country when he is expostulated with for making these charges without giving these men an opportunity to answer. And he has a number of gentlemen around him who were shocked because the other day tlie hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) was not disposed to give the name of a gentleman who had informed him that Mr. Win. Pugsley had gone to New York. These gentlemen almost wept with sorrow and grief over that refusal. Yet the hon. gentleman and his colleagues and his friends have nothing to say when an explanation is asked with regard to this extraordinary occurrence. Fifty or sixty or perl laps a hundred enumerators-I do not know the number-are charged deliberately in this House witli fraud of a most serious character, with perjury, with violating their oaths of office, and yet tlie Minister of Agriculture says that the only excuse he has for making these charges against these men behind their backs and without giving them tlie slightest opportunity to answer, is that the charges are true and the men must be such scoundrels that there is no use in asking them about the facts. I am surprised that the hon. gentleman should venture to rise in this House when he has no better explanation than that. I venture to think that it would have been far better for him to have retained his seat, to have said nothing at all, than to give so useless an explanation of his conduct as he has given. I deeply regret, for the sake of this country, that these gentlemen, members of this government, should have so little regard for tlie decency of civilized life as to make these charges against\ the public officers without giving them the slightest opportunity to be heard in their own behalf, without even speaking to these men before the charges were made thus publicly in this House. Why, the position taken by tbe Minister of Agriculture is a monstrous one. The charges that he made were not supported by any evidence under oath, they were supported by hearsay evidence statements made, in many cases, by persons Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
who did not pretend to speak from their own personal knowledge of the facts. The statements were not made under oath, but the returns made by these officers which are called in question, were made under oath. The work of these men was in discharge of their duty as public officers, and surely any man who undertakes to perform service for the country is at least entitled to expect that members of the government under whom he serves, or of any future government, will not attack him behind his back as has been done in this case, will not accuse him of fraud without at least giving him an opportunity of being heard in ills own defence.
Who was tlie chief census officer in 1891 ?
Mr. George Johnson.
Is he still in the employ of tlie government V
Yes.
Was he asked for any explanation of these alleged discrepancies, or called upon to make any report as to l ow they arose ?
He has not been called upon for such * report yet.

And he is still in the employ of the country, and occupying a responsible position. He was responsible to the government of that day and to the people of tlie country for tlie accuracy of the statements that were made ns to the results of the census of 1891. As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden. Halifax) has pointed out, most serious charges have been made by the hon. minister (Mr. Fisher) and one of his colleagues impugning the integrity of the enumerators in many places. Yet the gentleman who was responsible for the census and who is still a government officer has never been asked to give his views or to offer any explanation of what would appear to be very grave discrepancies in the census. Hon. gentlemen opposite have made so many statements within the last three or four years as to the progress Canada was making, as to the exodus being stopped, and as to the population of Canada increasing by leaps and bounds, that when the result of the census of 1901 was made known they had to find some pretext to justify their statements. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) in 1898 estimated the population of Canada at. five and three quarter millions, and expressed tlie hope that it would soon be six millions. But when the census figures were made known and tlie hon. gentleman found that he was wide of the mark, he devoted all the energy and ability he posmesses to pouring vituperation upon those who had taken the census ot 1891.
Did lie not give pretty good evidence for what he said ?

Not a particle of evidence that would be accepted by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) himself as a professional man. Not one single allegation was buttressed with statements under oath from those who knew the facts. It was ungenerous and unjust for a minister of the Crown to charge these officers with fraud and perjury and with giving false returns of the *census of ten years ago. But the extraordinary spectacle is presented to us to-night of the Minister of Agriculture having still in the employment of the Crown in his department the man who must have been responsible for this loose condition of things, if it existed. Surely he should have been treated as an honourable man, and if these inaccuracies had been discovered, as alleged, he should have been asked for an explanation of them ? He surely might have been invited to consider whether the statements as to frauds were correct or not and to say whether the figures presented in 1891 in connection with the census were worthy of credence or not ?
He might have been asked to explain the knitting factories and the carpet factories shown in the census of 1891.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cowan) will say something germane to the subject betore you. Mr. Chairman, I shall be happy to discuss it. I can only hear something about * knitting factories,' and I do not see what that has to do with the question. We have here a most humiliating state of affairs. Hon. members ot this House occupying the most responsible positions in Canada, ministers of the Crown, have not hesitated to make statements in this House which their friends in the country will be expected to believe, but which statements have not, so far, been justified by such evidence as to make them appeal-statements which can be relied upon as well founded. Is it the intention of the Minister of Agriculture to give Mr. Johnson an opportunity to explain, to call Mr. Johnson to liis aid in making an explanation of the discrepancies which are said to have been found in these various towns and parishes ? Would it not be reasonable to ask Mr. Johnson for an explanation ? If that gentleman is still worthy of being retained in the public service, surely he is the man who should be asked to account, if he can. for these alleged discrepancies ?

I have not come to any conclusion as to what steps I shall take in the further investigation of the census of 1891. As I said on a former occasion when this question was
discussed, this whole investigation arose out of a desire to check the census of 1901, and was carried on for that purpose, and with that object in view. The developments are shown by the papers laid on the Table of the House. As head of the bureau of statistics in 1891, no doubt Mr. Johnson is responsible for the census. But I have not suggested in any way that Mr. Johnson was responsible for these inaccuracies. All the evidence points to the fact that the enumerators in the different localities put on names for the purpose of swelling the returns. It has been suggested, though that may not be the proper explanation, that, as they were paid according to the names they put on, they sought to get more pay than they otherwise would. I have not gone Into that question, and have no results except those that I have laid on the Table. But I think these documents fully justify me and my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in the conclusions we drew that the census of 1S91 was materially and very largely stuffed in those counties in which we have had an investigation.

My dear Sir,-I have completed the work in ci r niection with the examinatiin of ihe census of 1891 for the Townhip of Thurlow and the city of Belleville, as requested by you.
I could have done the work much more quickly and easily had the numbers of the lots and concessions, ao well as the names of the streets been given. The decrease of population in' the township of Thurlow is attributable to two chief causes, first, the general movement to the unsettled parts of the Dominion and secondly to the fact that no work is being done at either of the large limestone quarries at Foxboro and Point Ann, where, ten years ago, fully six hundred inhabitants were directly dependent upon this industry. The money which was spent in that investigation was spent properly and rightly in dealing with the census of 1901 ; it was spent for the purpose of finding out whether the census of 1901, as it was taken by our enumerators, was correct. The first thing that struck us in the census of 1901 was that, in certain parts of Canada, there was a decrease of population as compared with the census of 1891. That seemed an extraordinary condition of affairs. Possibly there might have been some mistake in the census taking of 1901. We therefore took means to check over the census taken in 1901 and in that process of checking over the census we took the parochial returns in those constituencies where the population is practically altogether Catholic and consequently where the parochial returns would include practically the whole population. We found that in 21 of these counties there was a difference of 8,000 between the parochial returns and
the Dominion census returns of 1891. I may say that at the same time that was done the parochial returns of 1891 were consulted to see what the comparison was between them and the census returns of that year. The result was that we found in the parochial returns that there were a lot of names, but not by any means all of the names that were in the census and we found that the census contained numerically names that were not in the parochial returns. The question was to find out whether these census returns were correct, to find out whether the people enumerated in the census returns were there or not, and whether a mistake had occurred in the parochial returns or the census returns, and we found, on the evidence of men who knew these parishes through and through and year after year, many years before 1891. that there were people who were enumerated in the census but not in the parochial returns who were not present in these parishes and were not present when the census was taken. That was the object of the investigation. It was not an investigation to prove that the census of 1891 was incorrect but it was for the purpose of proving that the census of 1901 was and . is correct, and I think it is proved beyond peradventure, and if as a result of this investigation it has been found that the census taken toy hon. gentlemen opposite in 1891 was false and was stuffed, so much the worse for them and so much the worse for the way in which their census was taken. It was also proved that the Dominion of Canada has not been standing still, as it was thought to have been when the census returns first came out, but that, as a matter of fact, probably has increased in population at as fair a rate as could be fairly expected. The hon. gentleman speaks of this being a misappropriation of funds. As a matter of fact it was a perfectly proper expenditure for the purpose of proving that the census of 1901 was correct and was properly taken.
