speechtext: Perhaps the minister will hear later on something different. There are numerous claims by enumerators here averaging from $1 up to $56. My information is that all these gentlemen were settled with previous to the Lisgar election, and that the cheques were sent to them for these balances either in the month of January or February.
That information is entirely incorrect.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Well, perhaps we will have a way of reaching it.
I will give the hon. gentleman the stub cheque books, and if he can find there that payment was made to any one in Lisgar in Januarv or February, I will take back everything I have said.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is one statement in the list' of documents laid on Mr. TAYLOR.
the Table of the House which I would like to inquire about. One of the officers of the department says :
The object of procuring the parochial statistics was, first, to ascertain the correctness and accuracy of our own census ; and incidentally we discovered that the census of 1891 had been unduly stuffed, and made a thorough investigation in a few counties here and there throughout Canada.
I would like to inquire what meaning the hon. gentleman attaches to the expression ' unduly stuffed.' To what extent would the census have to be stuffed before it was unduly stuffed ?

I should say myself that if it were stuffed at all it would be unduly stuffed. What was meant was that there were names improperly entered in the census of 1891, because the people were not in the country when the census was taken.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What were the counties in which a thorough investigation was made ?
The list was placed on the Table. There were twenty-one counties In the province of Quebec in which the parochial returns were examined.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I inquire whether the hon. gentleman acquiesces in the view of his officer that that constitutes a thorough investigation ?

Yes, I think it is a thorough investigation to take the counties eminently entirely Catholic, and to check the census returns with the parochial returns in those counties. We took practically all the counties in the province of Quebec where that was the case.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: But this is a general statement, that the census of 1891, not in those particular counties, but in all the counties of Quebec at least, was unduly stuffed.

I think what we found in those counties would justify the statement that very generally the census of 1891 was unduly swelled by the insertion of the names of people who were not there. I referred on another occasion to a statement made on the floor of this House in 1S94 by hon. friend the Minister of Militia (Hon. Mr. Borden) as to what occurred in the province of Nova Scotia in his county on that occasion, and I think the accumulation of evidence is such as to justify the statement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: In other words the hon. gentleman thinks he is justified in accusing the enumerators in every county in Canada in 1891-

Not in every county.

Mr. 150III)EX (Halifax). In what counties, then, was the census of 1891 not unduly stuffed 7

I cannot tell in what counties the census was honestly taken and in what counties it was not, but we have evidence to show that in a large number of counties there was clear dishonesty in entering the names of people who were not in the country, and that being the case, I made the general statement.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says he has sufficient evidence on which to make a general statement that the census of 1891 was unduly stuffed, whatever that means. What I want to know is whether his information is sufficiently definite to enable him to state whether there is any county to be excepted from that statement. If there is, I would like him to name that county.

The hou. gentleman has just heard the statement read by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor), a statement to which I referred the other evening that the investigation in the town of Belleville and the township of Thurlow showed that the census there was accurately and properly taken. That is the only statement I have received, to show that in any particular place the census was accurately taken. I must correct myself in saying that. I am informed that there were reports laid on the Table from some counties which showed that the census was accurately taken in those counties. I cannot give the names of the counties at this moment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are not the hon. gentleman's officers prepared to give us the names of those counties ?
I have not got those names in my mind at the moment. The list was laid on the Table with the full statement in regard to them.
With regard to these parochial returns were they asked from the Roman Catholic clergymen of Prince Edward Island ?
No, we made no investigation in the province of Prince Edward Island at all.

In listening to the statements in this House regarding the conduct of the census enumerators in 1891, what they had done and what they had not done, one would readily come to the conclusion that human character was either of very little value in Canada, or that the moral code of some gentlemen in the country was at a very low ebb, because the freedom with which sweeping statements have been made regarding a large number of enumerators, extending to some thousands, that
they were practically perjurers, and had done what, if established in court, would land any one of them behind the bars of the penitentiary, is something astounding ; and when one comes to analyse the evidence on which these statements are made, one is forced to the conclusion that the parties who made them either had very little regard for men's characters or very little idea of what they were saying. I have in my hands one of these returns. It is from the town of Simcoe, and I give it as a fair sample of the others, though I have not gone over many of them. It is in just such returns that the statement was made in this House that these men had deliberately perjured and forsworn themselves. Mr. H. G. Petrie, of Simcoe, says :
The lapse of time and the consequent lapse of memory of persons having knowledge of the facts has rendered it very difficult to get information ; but notwithstanding this the list contains 120 names of persons improperly enumerated-77 in Simcoe and 43 in Port Dover- which alone instead of a decrease would have shown an increase compared with the returns of 1901.
He goes on and gives a number of these names, but the significance of the matter is that he nearly always speaks of them as being out of the place two years previous to the time the census was taken. He can manage to establish that data from the memory of people living in the locality, no matter how imperfect it is, with sufficient care to say that they were absent two years from the place or never lived in it. Then he goes on to say where he has given many of these names, that they were names of parties living in some other locality, but he is innocent enough to give himself away by saying that the names entered in the various schedules have not corresponded with many of the names. When he is giving duplicate names to show that the parties were taken in two places, he says the names do not correspond. That is sufficient to satisfy any person that the chances are that they were not the same parties at all. Although the names are the same, they were names of different individuals living in different localities.
He was depending on what was told him by people who were trying to charge their memory hack with conditions that existed ten years before. What hou. member cau say who resided ten years ago in the particular village or town in which that hon. member happens to be living ? How many of us could say on oath whelther such an individual lived ten years ago in our own town or not, or how long such an individual had been out of the place previous to 1891 '! In my opinion, had these people been put upon oath and questioned carefully and reminded that the information they were giving was information which was going to damn some people's character, they would have been much more careful. They were probably not aware of what use would be

made of the information they were giving, or they would have been much more careful. If we consider the lapse of time,, ten years, we must conclude that it would be very difficult for any one to say who were living in a certain place ten years ago. He might remember some of the prominent families or his associates in business and social relations, buit a great many other people he would utterly fail to recollect. And supposing he could remember that some were out of the place ten years ago, how could he tell how long they had been out of it, and whether they intended to come back or remain permanently away. We must not forget that in the Instructions given, the enumerators were ordered to enumerate any people who had left the place temporarily and were expected back. My attention was drawn to this in 1891 by a gentleman from the province of Quebec, who told me that this regulation would lead to an incorrect taking of the census. The enumerator puts the question to the head of a family : How many children have you ? The head of the family replies, so many, and gives the names. Then the enumerator asks of each :	Is he at home ? The head of the
family replies :	No. Then he puts the
question :	Do you expect him back ? And
in forty-nine cases out of fifty, especially iu the province of Quebec, the parent will reply iu the affirmative, even though the child had been away for years, and had married or settled down elsewihere. It is a fact that the heads of French Canadian families, iu nearly every instance, expect their children back. So that many names would go down in the census of people who were not in the locality at the time the census was taken and who did mot come back as was expected. Then the instructions go on to say that if the party is absent for a long time and the answer is not given that he is expected back, the enumerator must put this other question :	Has the
party been away over two years ? If an answer be given in the affirmative, his name is not taken down. But you can see how easy it would be for parties to be taken down, when the first question was answered in the affirmative, and how easy it would be to have many members of the family enumerated although they were out of the country at the time. I only mention this as an illustration to show how easy it was to make an incorrect census, and to do so innocently and in the faithful discharge of duty, according to instructions given. Then an analysis , is made and the census is found not absolutely correct, according to the memory of men living in the locality ten years later, and on such statements these enumerators are declared to be perjurers who ought really to be in the penitentiary. The parties who make these allegations must have very little respect for their fellow men', when they make these charges in the wholesale way they do. Take some of Mr. SPROUL.E.
these as an illustration. I find the following statement: 'McBride left Simcoe permanently in 1891, and has . not lived here since.' How could the man who made that statement know it hat McBride had left prior to 1891 and toad left permanently ? And is it not possible that McBride's name was taken down, on the statement of his parent that he was coming back; and because he has not come back since, we are to assume, on the statement of a party who is looking back ten years, that the enumerator is a liar and a perjurer ? Is that evidence on which we should rely in order to damn any one's character ? The Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce ought t'o be ashamed of themselves when they make use of such statements to bolster up these flimsy charges. Here is another statement:	' James Bray, married, and not resident in Simcoe.' There is not a word said about the time. Yet this is taken as evidence that the enumerator did not do his duty. Here is another : ' George Bray, married, and gone permanently, not resident in Simcoe.' There is nothing said as to when he left Simcoe or how long he had been out of the place or whether he was there in 1S91 or not, but this is considered as evidence that the enumerator is a liar. Here is another statement :	' James Weston, permanently engaged out of town, and not resident in 1S91 or several years prior.' I took a number of other eases, and in every instance the party was declared not to have been a resident for two years before 1891. The statement is very specific with regard to the exact tame, notwithstanding the fact that the memory of the parties who gave the information may have been defective, and there is a strange coincidence in the fact that in nearly every instance two years is given as the length of time when the parties mentioned were absent prior to 1891. Here is another statement :	' George Kelly, employed permanently on the railway, with headquarters elsewhere than Simcoe, was away a year previous to 1891.' There is nothing to verify Ithe statement, but the statement is made simply on recollection going back ten years. How does the party know that this man had been away a year before 1891 ? Is his memory infallible V Is it not possible that he may be all wroug? Yet such statements as these are taken to prove that the enumerator was a Mar and perjurer. What can the Minister of Agriculture think of himself when he takes such flimsy evidence for the purpose of damning human character ? I never heard of anything so disgraceful, and find it difficult to believe ithat any one who considers himself an honourable man should lend himself to such unworthy proceedings.
A few moments ago I asked the Minister of Agriculture if these parochial returns had been asked for from Prince Edward Island ?
I understand the clergy in the province of Prince Edward Island were asked for these returns but only one was sent in.
A moment ago the hon. minister said Ithere were none sent in.
They were asked for, but only one was sent in, and that was from the Rev. Mr. Gallon.
That would be Bloomfield ?
I could not say whati parish.
What township ?
I cannot give that information just now.
It appears that out of a large number, seventy-nine, he was the only one that made any reply. I would like to know what part of the island he resides in 1
Were the enumerators in Prince Edward Island appointed by townships or by polling divisions ?
The enumerators everywhere were appointed by polling divisions.
Who was the enumerator in the first polling division in West Prince ?
The memorandum does not show for which polling divisions the several enumerators were appointed. But if the hon. gentleman will give me any name he wishes to cheek-
A man called Doyle.

The hon. gentleman spoke of him the last time this item was under discussion, and I have obtained the information he desired. Doyle was appointed one of the enumerators, but when he was asked to take the oath, he declined to do so. The commissioner recommended Anthony Broderick as enumerator, and, on reference here, Broderick was appointed. He did the work and received the money.
Is the hon. minister aware that Doyle went around two days taking the .census ?
On the contrary, my information is that Broderick did the whole of the work. The books show that all the returns were made by Broderick and that the money was paid to him.

I happen to come from that county and I know all the facts. Doyle went about for a day or two taking the census, but found that he was incompetent and looked around for another man to take his place. Peter Broderick was anxious to get the job for his son, and Doyle offered for $20 to get him appointed. Broderick gave him $20 and got his son Anthony appointed, and he went around and took the census. It is difficult to say whether Broderick began where Doyle stopped or where he stopped himself.
But Doyle got the $20 ?
Yes, he did.

So far as the records of the department show, the commissioner there reported that Doyle, the man first appointed, refused to take the oath and the commissioner, Mr. Tweedy, recommended the appointment of Broderick. That was discussed here and the commissioner was authorized to appoint Broderick. The returns from the polling division are signed by Broderick and countersigned by the commissioner. Broderick received the money from the depart- [DOT] ment as having done the whole of the work. The cheque was made out In favour of Broderick. We have no knowledge whatever of Doyle having done any work in connection with the census. If the statement which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) makes is correct-and I have no doubt that he is convinced it is-'it has never come to our attention at all. If any farming out of the work has been done, it has been done in direct contravention of the instructions given to the commissioners and the enumerators, and we would not have recognized it. If, as the hon. gentleman says. Doyle did some of the work and (Broderick got paid for it, we know nothing of that here.
I am not finding fault with the minister in this connection, but I want to get at the facts. Will he please tell me who recommended Doyle and who recommended Broderick ?

I am informed that the recommendation of Doyle came from Mr. McLellan and Senator Yeo. When Doyle refused to take the oath Mr. Tweedy recommended Broderick. That was submitted to Sir Louis Davies, who was then a minister of the Crown, he endorsed it and Broderick was appointed.

I am pleased to get the information, and, as I say, I attribute nothing to the hon. minister in this connection.
I know the parties very weill. I was speaking with Doyle on my return from Ottawa last year. I had learned here that he was to be the enumerator. When I met him,
I said :	' Well, Martin, how are you getting along about the census.' He said :



' I am getting along fine; I have got $20 in my pocket that I got out of it, though I have only clone one or two day's work. I found it was a difficult undertaking, and I could not go ahead and take it, so, after working for a day or two I saw Peter Broderick and asked him if he would allow his son to do the work. And, I said : If you will give me $20, I will have your son appointed to take the census for the balance of the polling division.' So, it was accomplished in that way. If this kind of thing has been going on all over the Dominion, the hon. minister will see what an inefficient enumeration we have had. He will see that there must have been great looseness in the taking of the census. I am not finding fault with the minister, but simply pointing out the need for careful inspection in this work.

If anything of the kind the hon. gentleman speaks of has occurred elsewhere, of course it is something we know nothing about, and is directly contrary to the instructions given to all parties concerned. Of course, it could not have occurred had Broderick not been appointed. He was appointed [DOT] from here and it was supposed that he did the whole of the work. Broderick stands on our books as the enumerator for that polling subdivision, Doyle having disappeared in consequence of refusing to take the oath. That is the whole record in the department; therefore, there is no question so far as the department is concerned of any farming out of the work. If there was a bargain between Doyle and Broderick that Doyle should give up his work, or refused to take the work for a consideration from Broderick, that is a matter entirely outside the! knowledge or business of the department. I confess it is an improper thing, and should these gentlemen be referred to me again for employment, I would not employ them. I consider that farming out government work and traffic in offices is a most improper thing, and I should never allow it to be done by any of my officers, to my knowledge.
Atithony Broderick, then, was appointed solely on the responsibility of Mr. Tweedie, the commissioner, and not recommended by anybody else. Was he recommended by Mr. McLellan ?

No, he was recommended by Commissioner Tweedie, and that recommendation was endorsed by Sir Louis Davies. The appointment was made on that recommendation. I have just been informed that the parish of the reverend gentleman whose name I gave a few moments ago is Palmer Road.
That would be the Rev. Dr. Chaisson.

speechtext:

Pebruary. It commences December 21st, 1901. That is the only date I discover in the book; it runs on after that date until the end of the stubs. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Perhaps the minister can tell me who Geo. Coutts is, because the stubs of the cheque do not give any information at all except the name and the service.
I could not tell off-hand who Geo. Coutts is.

The MINISTER OP 'AGRICULTURE. I am informed this man was in the Atlin district, in the north of British Columbia, on the road to the Yukon.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext: How many names would an enumerator have to take to earn $1,198 ?	*
Those men were paid by the day. Men in the outlying districts, where they would have to cover a large extent of territory, were not paid by schedule rates.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I find there are three gentlemen; one received $1,198, Mr. Patrick received $758. and Harry E. Brown $643.
That, no doubt, is quite correct. The figures here are a little more. I suppose these cheques have been supplemented by others. Brown received $768, Geo. Coutts $1,216, and Robt. Patrick $800.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The cheque book gives practically no information. The hon. gentleman knew that, I fancy.
I gave the hon. gentleman the information on the statement which was made out by the accountant. .

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The statement shows there were balances.
That is the difference between the amount claimed by these enumerators when they sent their accounts in, and the amount allowed them under the schedule rates.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Do they still claim a balance ?
I cannot say whether it is still claimed or not. It was the difference between the original amount as sent in by the enumerators and the account as it was allowed in the department by the auditor.
Is there a further balance ?

Not unless there was some extraordinary reason, because the amount paid was fixed by schedule rates. There are a few instances where the difference may be legitimately paid if proof is supplied. For instance, the voucher may not be supplied with the .account at first, and if it is properly supplied afterwards the account would be paid. I cannot tell whether these balances are due to that or due to improper charges, for* too many names, for instance, or too many farms, or something of that kind. The accounts of the enumerators in every case have been carefully checked over. I regret to say that a large proportion of them, I daresay more than half of all the accounts sent in by all the enumerators have had to be cut down materially, and have been so settled. In some cases the settlement thus awarded is accepted, in other cases the enumerators send in statements afterwards which show that in some cases the reduction had been improper, that is to say, they had a proper account if they had supplied it in proper-form, and with the propel* vouchers and explanations. In those cases, where that is clearly shown, the difference would be paid, but not unless the account was shown to be in strict consonance with the regulations and schedule rates.

Perhaps their statements would be about as accurate as those of the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall this item be adopted ?
Is it understood the item should be held over ?
No, it is not understood.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word in reference to the matter that was mentioned in respect to which the hon. minister undertook to make the statement that the census of 1891 was dishonestly taken and stuffed with names of numerous persons who were not in the country. I think that the hon. minister has not at his command at present sufficient evidence to warrant him in making such a. statement. Apart from the fact that it would seem very improper to make a statement of that kind which involves the accuracy and honesty of most of the enumerators employed in 1891, I would be inclined to think that the hon. minister did not have at his command such evidence as would justify him in making that statement. He must rely upon evidence to make it and upon what evidence ? He simply says that certain statements are made to Mm by some individuals whom he has employed to revise the facts connected with the census of 1891. What reason has the hon. gentleman to attach more value or more importance to the statements given to him by the persons whom he has employed to revise the census of 1891 than he had to attach value to the figures givem by the enumerators at that time? Is it a certainty that all the enumerators employed by the commissioner, or the chief census officer who took the census in 1891, would be dishonest and that all the persons from whom the Hon. Mr. FISHER.
hon. minister obtained that information in the course of tMs present year would be absolutely honest ? It seems to me that there is no good ground advanced here to warrant the statement that has been made. Now, if it were true that sufficient evidence had been advanced to prove that the census of 1891, was a dishonest census, I think, unquestionably, the hon. minister would have proved the fact that a great wrong had been done to the country which had been deceived by a census which was dishonestly taken, and I would suppose in that case that the hon. minister would consider his duty not done until he had proceeded to punish, by reason of the power which the law gives him to punish the dishonesty in men who are employed by the country to do this work, any persons guilty of wrongdoing. If it be the truth that in the province of Quebec, in 21 counties, the enumerators, who must hiave been nearly all of the Roman Catholic faith, because we are told that the population was nearly all Roman Catholic-If it be the truth that in 21 counties of that province in 1891 the enumerators with one accord violated their oath and made false returns, I do not think the bon. minister will do himself justice until he proceeds to establish that fact by prosecuting these individuals in the courts. I do not see haw he can stop short of that. I think he should have bad that end iu view before he made the statement in public which he has made. I am sure that so far as a large part of the population of Canada is concerned, they will n*ever accept the statement made by the minister, or by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) for that matter, that they will not regard it as being of much weight, or as having been fully considered if the hon. minister do not proceed to vindicate the rights of the country and to punish these men who have done wrong, if they have done wrong. I would call attention to the fact that there cannot be much confidence attached to the investigation said to have been made by the hon. Minister of Agriculture. It is entirely ex parte and there is the further fact that what has always been looked upon as a binding rule in connection with the census has been clearly violated. The schedules of the census communicated to the enumerators and the officials of the country by the people under the seal of confidence, which is absolutely necessary m order to secure correct returns from the people who will not reveal their private affairs to any officials of the country unless they are satisfied that it is done in confidence, have been handed over to persons who apparently were not sworn to do exactly what was right and to act justly, or to maintain that secrecy which is necessary in order to secure the confidence of the people in that investigation. Why should the hon. minister assume. as he does assume, that all the officers'whom he has employed to make this in-

vestigation are absolutl.v correct, are absolutely honest, and that all the persons who were employed in 1891, under the chief census officer of that day, were absolutely dishonest ? Why should he ask this country and ask this committee to accept a statement prepared ten years after the facts, an ex parte statement, prepared by men not under oath and to believe that it should be more correct than a statement prepared in the regular official manner by the sworn enumerators and which was checked over by the chief census officers ? Why should the hon. minister, himself, believe such an absurd thing, and if he does believe it, why should lie ask the committee and the [DOT]country to believe such an obviously absurd story ? I think there could not be a more gross wrong done to these enumerators than to make this charge against them and then to leave It hanging in the position in which it now is. I believe it is due to these gentlemen that they should have this investigation now carried out to completion, that they should have it carried on carefully before a judge, or before an independent man, one who can command the confidence of both parties in the country, that all questions asked and all answers given should toe under oath and that such evidence should be adduced for the Use of the country as would command the confidence of every man in it.
It is well known to the Minister of Agriculture that the census of 1881 was supposed to be in excess of the actual facts, not on account of any intentional wrong doing, but because under the system whicli had been adopted, a great number of names of persons had been taken who were out of the country for more than one year, and in some cases for more than twenty years. It must be in the knowledge of the minister, that when the census of 1891 was taken, a new regulation was introduced in order to guard against that, and so far as the government of the day was concerned and so far as the officer who had charge of that census was concerned, they laid down a new proposition by which it was intended to avoid that error and to reduce the figures so that they would be more nearly accurate than the census of 1881. The result was what might have been expected ; that instead of the figures of 1891 showing such an increase over those of 1881 as might have been expected, the figures of 1891 were disappointing. Of course under the new rule a great many more names were excluded from the census of 1891 than in 1881, and the census of 1891 was more nearly correct. In the case of the census of 1901, simply because the growth of the country is less than these hon. gentlemen opposite expected, they proceeded without the authority of parliament, and in order as they alleged to vindicate the correctness of the census whicli they are now in process of making : they proceeded not to inquire into the correctness of the figures taken by their own officers-which they could have verified to a large extent because the circumstances are all fresh and the officers are living-but they proceeded to investigate the correctness of the census of 1891, relying upon the memory of persons as to facts eleven years old in order to test the correctness of the census made now. That is a most extraordinary course to pursue. The natural course would have been to have checked over the present census, or if they desired it to have checked both census. I am satisfied that no body of people in this country will accept the figures that have been given under such circumstances, as having the slightest value. I believe that the investigation should be continued, and that not only the census of 1891 but the census of 1901 should be investigated with all the solemnity of a court in a trial before a judge, and that we should in that way arrive at a nearly correct knowledge of the exact population of our country. That is a basic fact, and it is of the utmost importance that succeeding governments should know precisely the number of the people in Canada so as to mark the progress of the country. There are one of two circumstances toy which we can measure to some extent the character of the census of 1901. About the month of August, 1891, the chief census officer issued a statement of the population of Canada which agreed with the finally corrected statement as closely as one-quarter of one per cent ; an error only of some 2,000 persons. In the case of the census of 1901. in the month of January a statement was issued that the final determination of the figures was 5.369,666. but since that there has been another change made. It will be noticed that the census of 1891 was practically accurately and finally determined in four months after the census was taken, but in the census of 1901, ten months after it was taken and when we get the final result, we see that the first estimate shows an error about ten times as great as that which was made by the gentlemen who took the census of 1891, and the result of which was announced four months afterwards. This is a fact which is clear to us all, and it goes to show that there was more ability, and more care, and more thoroughness, and much more expedition shown in taking the census of 1891 than in taking the census of 1901. For that reason a great many persons in this country will continue to prefer to believe that the census of 1891 was a better census, cost less money, and was more quickly completed than the census of 1901. I do not suggest criminal wrong doing in connection with the census of 1901. but there are some circumstances in connection with that census which inspire a want of confidence in the people, and which were absent from the census of 1891. In the province of Nova Scotia there is, according to the census of 1901. but a very slight increase in the population. We find that increase entirely among the people of the

410S
French race in that province. If you take out of the census returns the increase shown in the few limited localities where people of the French race are to be found in Nova Scotia, you actually show a decrease in all the rest of the province. Now, to say the least, that is a highly improbable circumstance. It seems to me that in order to give the people of Canada confidence in the result of our census, it is not sufficient for the minister to make this partial, incomplete. and unsatisfactory investigation into the figures of 1891. but he should go on to make an absolutely thorough and exhaustive examination-not an expensive one-into the returns from some parts of the Dominion which will enable us to satisfactorily determine the result of the census of 1901, and which of course can be done much more thoroughly and much more satisfactorily than any inquiry into the census of 1891, which is now eleven years old. It has been suggested by the minister that there was a motive in 1891. I will not refer to the absurd suggestion made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) as to the reasons why all these enumerators in 1891 proceeded to make themselves criminals. But I shall refer to one reason given to-night by the Minister of Agriculture. He suggested that the enumerators in 1891 swelled the figures because they were paid for each name. But the minister must know that if that had any effect in 1891 it would have a hundred fold more effect in 1901. because he raised the price paid per name. Instead of paying 3 cents per name, as was done in 1891. the minister paid 5 cents per name in 1901. The minister must see that if 3 cents per name would increase the number unduly in 1891, the payment of 5 cents per name in 1901 would necessarily aggravate the error, if the error arose from that circumstance. I do not believe we have any reason whatever to conclude that men who are taken at random, selected by the different members of parliament to act as enumerators, could be found by a government that is bad enough to look for such characters, in such numbers as would be required to make all the enumerators of the Dominion of Canada absolute criminals and willing to obey the hint or nod of any government that is bad enough to require them to falsify the figures that they put down on their schedules. I would be sorry to think that it were possible that any one could believe that it is within the bounds of possibility that any government could, through the chief census commissioner, summon to its aid and service, thousands of formerly reputable men : men for the most part respected by their neighbours, who were willing to deliberately break an oath solemnly taken, and to repeat an act of perjury or falsification 500 times over; and to do that for what reason ? Simply because a political enemy suggests that the government of that day had a motive in securing a dishonest and impro-Mr. BELL.
per return from these enumerators. I think it is a terrible charge made against the people of Canada to insinuate that there is such a class of people among us, and that they are deliberately suggested by the representatives of the* people of Canada who sit in parliament, when those representatives are asked by the government to supply them with trusty men to take an honest census of the people. It is a most improper suggestion, and if it has been sincerely made by the minister, I think he owes it to himself, to his character and reputation in the country, to every enumerator, and to the chief census officials-because they are all involved-to give them an opportunity to disprove the charge, and to show that they have acted as honest men and worthy citizens. And I would suggest-and I hope the government will accept the suggestion-that having gone as far as they have gone to raise this question and to make this charge, through the mouths of two ministers, and I dare say a third-because the Minister of Finance seems to concur in the idea that the census of 3891 was exaggerated-having made this charge against an important section of the people of Canada, they owe it to their own reputations and to the men assailed to carry that investigation to the point of enabling any fair-minded man to determine whether there is anything beneath the charge or not.

I am glad in one way to have the endorsement of the hon. gentleman who has just sat down, of my course. He says I ought to have begun by investigating the accuracy of the census of 1901. That is exactly what I did, and what has led to all this discovery in regard to the census of 1891. The apparent anomaly which we discovered, that a large number of the rural districts of Canada had decreased in population between 1891 and 1901 according to the census returns of those years, led us to check our own returns of 1901 with the different parochial returns of the province of Quebec for 1901, and we found that they corresponded in a marked degree. We therefore believed that our census returns were correct. We then made a comparison of the parochial returns of 1891 with the census returns of 1891, and found such discrepancies that we had to believe that either the parochial returns of 1891 or the census of 1891 were inaccurate.

But the hon. minister did not proceed to do that in such a way as to divest the investigation entirely of partisan or government manipulation. It was done secretly. Would it not have been better to have put this investigation into the hands of a commission or a judge, so that the result would compel the acceptance of every one ?

The returns were taken as a purely departmental work. It was not done, as hon. gentlemen opposite seem to think it should have been done, by a special vote of parliament, outside of the census of 1901. It was done with the money voted for the work of the census, for the purpose of checking our returns and ascertaining whether they were correct or not. But we had to go the length we did go before we could prove it to a demonstration, and we believe that in the results which were found, which we were asked to lay on the Table, and which we have laid on the Table, it has been proved to a demonstration. Unfortunately this was not the first expose of the census of 1891. The hon. gentleman will remember that the hon. Minister of Militia of to-day, in 1894, brought up in this House the results of the census of 1891 in his county, the county of King's, N.S., and he proved conclusively at that time, by the list of names he was able to give, that the census of 1891 had been unduly swelled in that county.
In the case of one enumerator.

And he offered to go on and show that the same was the case generally in the county; but the hon. gentleman's own friends, sitting at that time on this side of the House, shut off the inquiry, and refused to give the information by .which he Could have shown it, because they knew perfectly well that if my hon. friend had been allowed to go on, he would have beeu able to show that it was general in his county.
I do not agree jvith that.

The hon. gentleman may not agree with the motive, but if he goes back to ' Hansard ' and other records of that day, he will find that the facts were as I have stated ; and the Minister of Militia, who is here, can corroborate me in that regard.
Hear, hear.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman says I ought to prosecute the men who did that work. I would ask him what his own friends did in the county of King's ?
They proceeded to prosecute the enumerator, and he left the country.
I am credibly informed that he did "not leave the country, but that two weeks later he was in an adjoining county.
That may be, but he left his own home.

He left his own home and went into an adjoining county, where my hon. friend's friends did not make any effort to find him or prosecute him.
The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND
DEFENCE. If I may be allowed to interrupt for a moment, I may say that the enumerator in question had moved from my county to Amherst before the matter was brought up here at all, and he has never left Amherst from that day to this.

It is even worse than I thought it was. The hon. gentleman's friends did not take much trouble to find him. They did not take the advice the hon. gentleman is now giving me, and prosecute this man, when they had the proof of what he had done.
He can be got at yet.

It is possible he can be, and I am not prepared to say that no step shall be taken against the gentleman who did this work. That is a question that has not been reached yet. I may say frankly that I do not think the end of this investigation is by any means reached yet. I am not prepared to make a statement to-night, but it is quite possible that this matter is of such importance that further steps may be taken, either in the courts or otherwise. But I want to point out the injustice of the hon. gentleman in taking me so severely to task for not prosecuting these men when his own friends did not attempt to prosecute this one enumerator who was within their reach, and has been for eleven years, and could have been prosecuted during all that time.
I think the hon. gentleman is a little unjust in allowing his bias to give one law for me and another for his own political friends and leader at that time. I do not wish to blame the hon. gentleman; but I think that under the circumstances he is taking a position which is hardly justified and which does not become him. As far as the investigation is concerned. I have pointed out that I did undertake to investigate the census of 1901, for which I was responsible, and in the province of Quebec, where the parochial returns were obtainable, the comparison showed, as far as it went, that the census of 1901 was accurate; and in going further with that same investigation. I found that a comparison of the parochial returns with the census of 1S91 showed that the census of 1891 was inaccurate.
I went further to find out the details and got those details-name after name, family after family, given in full and laid upon the Table of the House weeks ago. It is not a matter of making general statements, but a statement based on particular facts, which leaves no room for doubt. It may be necessary to have an investigation under oath, but that would be long, elaborate and expensive. Personally I would be glad to have such an investigation because I am

satisfied it would show clearly and distinctly that the census of 1901 was well taken and that the census of 1891 was unduly swelled in the way I have pointed out. That would be an endorsation of the work done by my department, but whether it would be worth while incurring the expenditure and taking the time, I am not prepared to say just now.
How is the census of the manufacturing establishments taken ?
The larger manufacturing centres were taken by special enumerators and the other places were taken by the ordinary enumerators.
Were the enumerators who took the manufactures appointed on the same principle as the general enumerators-on the recommendation of the defeated candidate or local member.
They were recommended In the same way as the others.
No special qualification required ?
It was understood what they were needed for.
What about the question of the fisheries ?
The fisheries were taken, as a general rule, by officers of the department of Marine and Fisheries.
Who took the census of the fisheries in the county of Charlotte ?

What amount was paid Mr. E. O. Callaghan, who makes a report with reference to the town and township of Cornwall ? I find here a report from him dated January 24th, which does not seem to convey much information to the Minister of Agriculture. Mr. Callaghan finds that a number of McPhails and McDonalds have been duplicated. I would call the ministers attention to the fact that in the township of Cornwall, which is settled largely by Scotchmen, there is a number of McPhails and McDonalds who have the same names, and it is quite possible that the enumerators in 1891 have got them quite correct. There is quite a reflection cast in this report on the enumerators of 1891.
I may say that I am familiar with the names of these enumerators. They are all men of good standing in the electoral district of Cornwall and Stormont, who, I am quite satisfied, would not duplicate names. This report, to my mind, is very indefinite. Mr. Callaghan winds up by saying that the list which is appended to his report shows that there were at least 150 persons whose names were duplicated by the enumerators of the district. It seems to me' Hon. Mr. FISHER.
that these names have not been duplicated. There are many McDonalds of the same name and many McPhails and many Lapointes of the same name. I would like to know what has been paid Mr. Callaghan for this very indefinite report. I am quite satisfied that the enumerators in 1891 did their duty correctly and that there have been no errors in the census taken by them.

If the hon. gentleman will read the report carefully he will find that Mr. Callaghan refers to that very fact. He says that there were a great many people of the same name, but he took particular pains to put in that list of 150 names those he knew perfectly well were duplicated.

I think the hon. gentleman is wrong in his construction of that report. That is not what Mr. Callaghan says, what he says is this : ' I do not therefore pretend that my inquiry has been full or exhaustive.' Then he goes on to point out the great difficulties in coming to any conclusion as regards the town and township of Cornwall, owing to the fact that there ai-e many McDonalds and McPhails and many of the other names mentioned in the list. I wish to ascertain the remuneration paid Mr. Callaghan as comrnis-ioner for this report.

His account has not been sent in yet and nothing has been paid him. I may inform the hon. member for' Charlotte that Mr. Patrick McLaughlin of St. John took the fishery enumeration in Charlotte county.
On whose recommendation was Mr. McLaughlin appointed ?
I think the gentleman who opposed the hon. member in the last election.
What pay did he receive ?
That account just covers one fishery district I believe ?
Yes.
Have the returns been published ?
No, they are in but have not yet been tabulated.

This is just an illustration of what I said the other night. We could have furnished the minister down there with all the Reformers he needed to take the census in New Brunswick, and in the selection of this gentleman I must say that, of all the Reformers in the county, he was the least fitted for the work. We have in that county one of the most. important

fisli industries in the maritime provinces, and why the minister did not send a man qualified for that position to take the fishery census is what I cannot understand. This man at one time drove a mail and I know not what else he has done. There is not a man less qualified than he to take the fishery census in that county. The minister had good officers there, men who had been fishery overseers, who could tell pretty well whether the fishermen were giving correct statements or not. Why were none of these appointed. But instead we had a man appointed who formerly drove a mail to take the census of the most important industry in Charlotte. I certainly think that if you get the report from the gentleman and compare it with this blue book you issue here, you will find that you have made a mistake in his appointment. I have consulted several gentlemen in the fishery business and it has been a perfect marvel to them that any such appointment should have been allowed to have been made by the department. In fact, I think that the information he would get from some of those engaged in the business would be very meagre. One gentleman said he did not propose to tell his business to an old woman who would report it all over the county. That is the opinion that the fishermen generally have of the census commissioner in that county. If the census of the fisheries business for the Dominion generally is taken like that in this county I think it will show very poor results for the business.

Of course I do not know the gentleman personally, nor what his qualifications are. He was recommended as qualified for the position, and I aim informed by my officer that the returns he sent in are in good order, 'and look as if the work had been carefully and accurately done. Until the results can be tabulated and checked over, we cannot tell much more about the matter. I did not know whether he was a farmer or a [DOT]mail driver. But I can understand that a man who carries the mail through the *county would be pretty well acquainted With the people and with the business that 'is being carried on

' Mr. GANONG. He does not drive the mail over the fishing waters.
'No, but he drives along the highway where the people live who carry on the fisheries. As I say, I do not know the gentleman or his qualifications.
I would like to ask the minister if it is his intention to stop when this item is passed ?

No. But there is an item for the census in the supplementary estimates, and on the discussion oiSthat item any of these questions can be taken up and any information
that is desiied given. But, as this item is the last one that I have in the main estimates, I think it should be passed to-niight.

I have taken very little part in "the debate, but 1 have listened attentively to what has been said by others. I must say that, regarding it with as little bias as possible, it looks as if this census business was to a great extent being made the ground of party conflict in this country. I heard the discussion in this House about the census of 1891. The debate was carried on at great length. And, as I say, the same accusations that are heard upon this side of the House were made by bon. gentlemen opposite who were then in opposition. But the importance of the question involved in this census can hardly be exaggerated. It has been shown that the present census will cost more than twice as much as did the census of 1891, and counties have been named in which, although there are fewer people than there were ten years ago, the cost of taking the census is double what it was then. Observing the minister as he made his explanations, I feel sure that he was not able to explain to his own satisfaction. For, whatever opinion I may have of the hon. gentleman politically, I believe lie does like to be able to explain things to his own satisfaction. In fact, I never knew a mau to take greater delight in explanation than the hon. minister does. But he has not been able to please himself, I am sure, with his explanation of the enormous expense that has been incurred in the present census. As regards the county of Lisgar, which has been a good deal discussed, the information I gave was from men who saw the cheques in that county, cheques which were issued to straighten up the accounts of men who bad not, up to that time, been able to get their accounts settled, but who had no difficulty in doing so in the warfare that went on there in the by-election. I did not see these cheques myself, I would be very much surprised to find that the hon. minister would lend himself to such dealings as was indicated by my informants. But at the same time, I do not know how to disbelieve or disregard the facts that were given to me. This item has; been a good deal discussed, and, if bon. gentlemen on this side are satisfied to let it go, provided that there is another item on which we can get any further explanation that may be desired, I, for my part, would be willing to have it pass. The right hon. premier, who was peacefully slumbering a short time ago, has wakened up. And, as he is to represent us soon upon a very important occasion, and as we desire that he should leave here in perfect health, I should be glad not to have him detained here very much longer. If the right bon. gentleman [DOT]promises to ad.iourn the House after the [DOT]passing of this item, I, for my part-though *of course, I do not speak with any authority -would be disposed to consent to its passing.

This report has only 'been placed in my hands this moment. But, having glanced at it, I must say I find it *somewhat surprising and would like to ask one or two questions in connection with it. 1 do not wish to cast any reflection on the commissioner, Mr. O'Callaghan. That gentleman, I believe, attended the convention at which I was nominated, and he was then seeking the Conservative nomination, but is now, I believe, a very active Liberal in the local contest. I do not know exactly why be should have been converted so suddenly. But he has a perfect right to change his politics, if he so desires. But he says in this report:
There were hundreds oi persons employed at the time on the canal work who lived in temporary hoarding houses along the canal, of whom there is no record except the pay sheets of the contractor and the schedules of the census.
Then he winds up his report by saying be thinks there have been some 150 duplicated. He casts reflections upon men who stand very high in the electoral districts of Cornwall and Stormont, and I cannot allow this report to pass without saying a word. The men who were enumerators in the township of Cornwall stand very high in that township. I do not know what their polities are. Bbt when he mentions men in the township of Cornwall like Mr. T. J. McDonald and Mr. McLaughlin, and men in the town of Cornwall like Mr. Broderick, Mr. Shaver and Mr. Buteau ; and men in the township of Pinch like Mr. McNaugta-ton and Mr. Wood, I would be recreant in my duty if I allowed to pass without protest a report casting reflections upon gentlemen who stand so high in that community. Mr. Callaghan, I must say, is very indefinite in this report. He says he thinks there are about 150 persons whose names were duplicated by the enumerators ; but he admits in another clause of the report that it was utterly impossible for him to say whether these enumerators were right or wrong, as a large number of these people have left the locality since 1891 who had been employed in connection with public works, or on the Cornwall canal. I would like to ask the minister upon whose recommendation Mr. Callaghan was employed. Was it upon the recommendation of Mr. Mulhern, the Liberal candidate at the last election ?

I think Mr. Callaghan was recommended by Mr. .T. F. Mulhern. I would like to say in regard to that report-which I would like the hon. gentleman to send over to me if he would-that the two parts of the report which he says are conflicting, to my mind do not conflict at all. Mr. Callaghan says distinctly there was a large number of people on the lists who were probably canal employees and who passed away ; but there is nothing in his report to indicate that any Mr. BOYD.
of the 150 names which he mentions as being duplicated were of that class. Mr. Callaghan declares distinctly that these 150 were people about whom he knows, and were not of the class which he refers to in the other part of the report as people about whom he could not say anything. So I think that what the hon. gentleman calls an inconsistency in his report is on the contrary a confirmation of the report, and shows that what Mr. Callaghan does state he states it with positive knowledge. In the other part of the report he acknowledges there were many people there besides these 150 about whom he could not give information. He says the list which is appended shows there were at least 150 persons whose names were duplicated by the enumerators of the district, and at least ten others were recorded who were domiciled elsewhere, who were not in the place when the census was taken.

If the hon. gentleman will look through the list of names there he will find McPhails and McDonalds. We have any number of McPhails and McDonalds, not only in the town of Cornwall, but in the township of Cornwall.

I fully endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) that the minister is endeavouring in every, possible way to satisfy the committee with regard to bis estimates. I believe he is perfectly conscientious in what he is saying to us. I would like to ask the minister -who was appointed for taking the fishery census for Prinefe county, Prince Edward Island ?
Tohn Davidson, of Bedeque.
What was his salary and travelling expenses ?
He was paid on the whole $184.25. I have not a statement of how much his travelling expenses were. Pie was paid at the rate of $3 a day for the time he worked.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: And $1.50 for horse hire ?
For all expenses, provided they showed vouchers for the accounts.
Mr. Davidson is a very competent man, I think he is all right, but lie is a fishery officer.

I think all the men who took the census in Prince Edward Island were fishery officers except one.
Geological Survey, $64,430.
Might I ask who is the head of this department now ?

There has been no

permanent director appointed yet. Dr. Bell, as senior officer of the survey, is the acting director.
speakername: The MINISTER OP THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

speechtext: Is there any prospect of an appointment at an early date ?

I think the appointment will be made in a few months.
Dominion lands-chargeable to income, $157,-5$2.
Will there be some supplementary estimates in regard to Dominion lands ?

I will have a vote on which my hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) may speak if he wishes.
Superintendence of insurance-to meet expenses in connection with this service, $11,500.

This is an item which properly speaking is not a charge against the Dominion treasury as it is recouped to us by the insurance companies. There is a readjustment of salaries and statutory increases in two or three cases so that there is nothing special about it.
Maintenance of assay office at Vancouver, $16,000.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) if it is his intention to establish an assay office at Dawson ?

We have no positive intention in regard to that, but I may say to my hon. friend that the question of establishing an assay office at Dawson would depend largely on the time that the mint gets into operation so that we could buy the gold ourselves. I am under the impression that as soon as the mint is in working order we will probably require an assay office at Dawson, although I cannot speak positively about it as yet.

It has been the opinions of the trade, and of merchants generally, both on the coast and in Dawson, that the establishment of an assay office there would be more beneficial to them than an assay oflite at Vancouver. It appears that they are obliged in trade to take gold at a valuation something in excess of what it is really worth, and there is great difficulty in establishing the value of it, because it cannot be ascertained in Dawson. It has been and is the occasion of a very considerable loss to the traders there. They are at present taking gold dust at the value of $16 per ounce, and they find that when sent to the coast it does not realize more than $15 an ounce, and they have been memorializing the department to the effect that the establishment of an assay office at Dawson would enable them to handle the gold at its actual value. The banks could purchase it, or traders might remit the gold bars instead of
remitting the dust, and they would be able to ascertain the actual value on the spot.
I noticed in the press only a short time ago that the traders of Dawson have recommended very strongly that an assay office should be established there, and established at as early a date as possible ?

I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Earle) that my information is much to the same effect as his own. The probability is that 'the miners are not receiving altogether full value for the gold. They propose, and I think in many ways it would be desirable, to establish an assay office there. I have discussed the matter very fully with Mr. Ross, the commissioner of the Yukon, who has been here for some time, and all I can say to my hon. friend is that the whole subject will receive very full and careful consideration.
Maintenance, construction, of roads, bridges and other necessary works in connection with the Hot Spring Reservation near Banff station, N.W.T., $19,420.
What is the meaning of that item ?

This is a general vote for the maintenance of the national park at Banff. It provides for taking care of the buildings, the museum, and the construction of roads which goes on to some extent all the time under the supervision of the superintendent. There is an increase of $5,000 this year which is to provide for the erection of a new building for the museum. The museum at present is very small and it is absolutely necessary to have a little more accommodation. The museum is one of the things that attracts the attention of visitors.

Has the park been increased in size ?
The MINISTER OB' THE INTERIOR. Yes, the Bill for the increase of the size of tlie park received its third reading a couple of days ago. T.he park will now be about 5,000 square miles in extent.
Are there many visitors in the summer season ?
The number of visitors is so great that the Canadian Pacific Railway are enlarging their hotel by the addition of several hundred rooms in order to be able to accommodate them.

The number has very largely increased; in fact, the number was so great that during the last couple of months of the season the Canadian Pacific Railway had to send word ahead that visitors could not stop there because they had not any accommodation. As my hon. friend says, they intend to very largely increase the accommodation. It will be a matter of gratification to the House to know that the expenditure upon

this work has not been without effect in attracting visitors and has caused it to become very much more popular as a resort.

That is very satisfactory, and I am glad to hear it, because in the east a great many people say that this park is simply a pleasure ground for some of the government members. I am very pleased to hear that it is visited by a large number of people and that it is going to be a great success.

The park is becoming a place of very general resort for visitors who take the transcontinental trip. My recollection is that when I was there in December I w-as told that the visitors for the year numbered something over 13,000. That is a very large number, and they generally remain a considerable length of time. "
Department of the Interior-Cost of litigation, $1,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: When the Liberals were in opposition they charged the Conservatives with wasting this money and not employing the Solicitor General to do the work. Now we have a Solicitor General and a Minister of Justice, and the Liberals are not doing what they promised.

This is not much.
Department of Labour, $34,900.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Will there be an item for this in the supplementaries, or the further supplementaries, or the further further supplementaries, because if not I will ask it to stand.
The MINISTER uF FINANCE. I think there will. At all events, I will give my hon. friend a guarantee that he will have an opportunity of raising the question.
Printing Bureau-Plant, 5 Linotyoe machines, $15,000

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: With this new machinery will the Printing Bureau be able to do all our printing. Large sums have been paid to outside newspapers and others to do the printing, and even some of the departmental reports have been printed in that way. Surely the Printing Bureau ought to be able to do ail the printing of the government without employing the Montreal 'Herald ' and other newspapers.

I do not know that I can guarantee what my hon. friend desires, but with this additional equipment we certainly can do more and there will be less occasion to go outside.
Cost of arbitration respecting the accounts between the Dominion of Canada and the provinces of Ontario and Quebec (payments on account of services rendered may bo made to members of the Civil Service, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act), $3,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is this arbitration going to sit for ever ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: I do not wonder that my hon. friend asks that because it has sat for several years longer than I imagined. We are doing everything possible to have it closed up, and I think it possible that at no distant date we will succeed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Has any return been made of tbeir work ?
A statement is made every year as to how the matter stands.
How often do the arbitrators meet ?

They are judges in the different provinces and they cannot meet always at our convenience. We have to consult their convenience and also the convenience of the provinces, all of which means slow progress. We have so little now to take up in the main estimates that -we might finish them to-night. The Minister of Trade and Commerce Is not present, but these estimates are not in any case increased, and that being the case, we might pass them, and there will be in tbe supplementaries some items relating to that department, so that if there is anything that requires notice hon. gentlemen will have an opportunity of bringing it up.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The leader of the opposition may have something to say on some of these mail subsidy items, and we will call them carried if a promise is made that they can be discussed later on.
AVe will afford every opportunity for discussion at another stage.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is there anything in these estimates for the fast line V

Not at present. That will come in the further further supplementary estimates that my hon. friend has spoken of.
Some resolutions reported.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), who has been called away, requested me to ask when the return respecting passes on the Intercolonial Railway, the motion for which was passed in this House on the 6th March last, will be brought down.
I will inquire about It.
